entries.0e5ac3f4415ad4984c98fe76cbcc9d71c4e3aa66: <div sID="gen13575" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="10" osisID="Prov.10" sID="Prov.10"/> <div eID="gen13575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13576" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13577" type="x-p"/> Hitherto we have been in the porch or preface to the proverbs, here they begin. They are short but weighty sentences; most of them are distichs, two sentences in one verse, illustrating each other; but it is seldom that there is any coherence between the verses, much less any thread of discourse, and therefore in these chapters we need not attempt to reduce the contents to their proper heads, the several sentences will appear best in their own places. The scope of them all is to set before us good and evil, the blessing and the curse. Many of the proverbs in this chapter relate to the good government of the tongue, without which men's religion is vain.
entries.120bd752c84272d4e02116349ea493ac5211dd50: <div eID="gen13577" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13576" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Weighty Sayings.</title> <div sID="gen13578" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The proverbs of Solomon. A wise son maketh a glad father: but a foolish son <hi type="italic">is</hi> the heaviness of his mother. <div eID="gen13578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13579" type="x-p"/> Solomon, speaking to us as unto children, observes here how much the comfort of parents, natural, political, and ecclesiastical, depends upon the good behaviour of those under their charge, as a reason, 1. Why parents should be careful to give their children a good education, and to train them up in the ways of religion, which, if it obtain the desired effect, they themselves will have the comfort of it, or, if not, they will have for their support under their heaviness that they have done their duty, have done their endeavour. 2. Why children should conduct themselves wisely and well, and live up to their good education, that they may gladden the hearts of their parents, and not sadden them. Observe, (1.) It adds to the comfort of young people that are pious and discreet that thereby they do something towards recompensing their parents for all the care and pains they have taken with them, and occasion pleasure to them in the evil days of old age, when they most need it; and it is the duty of parents to rejoice in their children's wisdom and well-doing, yea, though it arrive at such an eminency as to eclipse them. (2.) It adds to the guilt of those that conduct themselves ill that thereby they grieve those whom they ought to be a joy to, and are a heaviness particularly to their poor mothers who bore them with sorrow, but with greater sorrow see them wicked and vile.
entries.d37232b4839c30b2d3cbb5c97cc12ff0a0f04312: <div eID="gen13579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13580" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> Treasures of wickedness profit nothing: but righteousness delivereth from death. <hi type="super">3</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will not suffer the soul of the righteous to famish: but he casteth away the substance of the wicked. <div eID="gen13580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13581" type="x-p"/> These two verses speak to the same purport, and the latter may be the reason of the former. 1. That wealth which men get unjustly will do them no good, because God will blast it: <hi type="italic">Treasures of wickedness profit nothing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.10.2">v. 2</reference>. The treasures of wicked people, much more the treasure which they have made themselves masters of by any wicked people, by oppression of fraud, though it be ever so much, as a treasure, and laid up ever so safely, though it be hidden treasure, yet it <hi type="italic">profits nothing;</hi> when profit and loss come to be balanced the profit gained by the treasures will by no means countervail the loss sustained by the wickedness, <reference osisRef="Matt.16.26">Matt. xvi. 26</reference>. They do not profit the soul; they will not purchase any true comfort or happiness. They will stand a man in no stead at death, or in the judgment of the great day; and the reason is because God <hi type="italic">casts away the substance of the wicked</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.3">v. 3</reference>); he takes that from them which they have unjustly gotten; he rejects the consideration of it, not regarding the rich more than the poor. We often see that scattered by the justice of God which has been gathered together by the injustice of men. How can the treasures of wickedness profit, when, though it be counted substance, God casts it away and it vanishes as a shadow? 2. That which is honestly got will turn to a good account, for God will bless it. <hi type="italic">Righteousness delivers from death,</hi> that is, wealth gained, and kept, and used, in a right manner (righteousness signifies both honesty and charity); it answers the end of wealth, which is to keep us alive and be a defence to us. It will deliver from those judgments which men bring upon themselves by their wickedness. It will profit to such a degree as to deliver, though not from the stroke of death, yet from the sting of it, and consequently from the terror of it. For <hi type="italic">the Lord will not suffer the soul of the righteous to famish</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.3">v. 3</reference>), and so their <hi type="italic">righteousness delivers from death,</hi> purely by the favour of God to them, which is their life and livelihood, and which will keep them alive in famine. The soul of the righteous shall be kept alive by the word of God, and faith in his promise, when <hi type="italic">young lions shall lack and suffer hunger.</hi>
entries.293a3e4aac11bf36f82ffb35819b230dedd46c9e: <div eID="gen13581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13582" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> He becometh poor that dealeth <hi type="italic">with</hi> a slack hand: but the hand of the diligent maketh rich. <div eID="gen13582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13583" type="x-p"/> We are here told, 1. Who those are who, though rich, are in a fair way to <hi type="italic">become poor</hi>—those <hi type="italic">who deal with a slack hand,</hi> who are careless and remiss in their business, and never mind which end goes foremost, nor ever set their hands vigorously to their work or stick to it; those <hi type="italic">who deal with a deceitful hand</hi> (so it may be read); those who think to enrich themselves by fraud and tricking will, in the end, impoverish themselves, not only by bringing the curse of God on what they have, but by forfeiting their reputation with men; none will care to deal with those who deal with sleight of hand and are honest only with good looking to. 2. Who those are who, though poor, are in a fair way to become rich—those who are diligent and honest, who are careful about their affairs, and, what their hands find to do, do it with all their might, in a fair and honourable way, those are likely to increase what they have. <hi type="italic">The hand of the acute</hi> (so some), of those who are sharp, but not sharpers; <hi type="italic">the hand of the active</hi> (so others); the stirring hand gets a penny. This is true in the affairs of our souls as well as in our worldly affairs; slothfulness and hypocrisy lead to spiritual poverty, but those who are <hi type="italic">fervent in spirit, serving the Lord,</hi> are likely to be <hi type="italic">rich in faith</hi> and <hi type="italic">rich in good works.</hi>
entries.223a08be92943f61f993d830dd1fac3393ef92d6: <div eID="gen13583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13584" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> He that gathereth in summer <hi type="italic">is</hi> a wise son: <hi type="italic">but</hi> he that sleepeth in harvest <hi type="italic">is</hi> a son that causeth shame. <div eID="gen13584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13585" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The just praise of those who improve their opportunities, who take pains to gather and increase what they have, both for soul and body, who provide for hereafter while provision is to be made, who <hi type="italic">gather in summer,</hi> which is gathering time. He who does so <hi type="italic">is a wise son,</hi> and it is his honour; he acts wisely for his parents, whom, if there be occasion, he ought to maintain, and he gives reputation to himself, his family, and his education. 2. The just reproach and blame of those who trifle away these opportunities: <hi type="italic">He who sleeps,</hi> loves his ease, idles away his time, and neglects his work, especially <hi type="italic">who sleeps in harvest,</hi> when he should be laying in for winter, who lets slip the season of furnishing himself with that which he will have occasion for, <hi type="italic">is a son that causes shame;</hi> for he is a foolish son; he prepares shame for himself when winter comes, and reflects shame upon all his friends. He who gets knowledge and wisdom in the days of his youth <hi type="italic">gathers in summer,</hi> and he will have the comfort and credit of his industry; but he who idles away the days of his youth will bear the shame of his indolence when he is old.
entries.b9d5b9e165f92402579221f9425229799a3a23eb: <div eID="gen13585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13586" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Blessings <hi type="italic">are</hi> upon the head of the just: but violence covereth the mouth of the wicked. <div eID="gen13586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13587" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. <hi type="italic">The head of the just</hi> crowned with <hi type="italic">blessings,</hi> with the blessings both of God and man. Variety of blessings, abundance of blessings, shall descend from above, and visibly abide on the head of good men, real blessings; they shall not only be spoken well of, but done well to. Blessings shall be on their head as a coronet to adorn and dignify them and as a helmet to protect and secure them. 2. <hi type="italic">The mouth of the wicked covered</hi> with <hi type="italic">violence.</hi> Their mouths shall be stopped with shame for the violence which they have done; they shall not have a word to say in excuse for themselves (<reference osisRef="Job.5.16">Job v. 16</reference>); their breath shall be stopped with the violence that shall be done to them, when their violent dealings shall return on their heads, shall be returned to their teeth.
entries.e770f2a044f0019ba4dbe98fc8cc2b8974f8816e: <div eID="gen13587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13588" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> The memory of the just <hi type="italic">is</hi> blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot. <div eID="gen13588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13589" type="x-p"/> Both the just and the wicked, when their days are fulfilled, must die. Between their bodies in the grave thee is no visible difference; between the souls of the one and the other, in the world of spirits, thee is a vast difference, and so there is, or ought to be, between their memories, which survive them. <div eID="gen13589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13590" type="x-p"/> I. Good men are and ought to be well spoken of when they are gone; it is one of the blessings that <hi type="italic">comes upon the head of the just,</hi> even when their head is laid. Blessed men leave behind them blessed memories. 1. It is part of the dignity of the saints, especially those who excel in virtue and are eminently useful, that they are remembered with respect when they are dead. Their good name, their name with good men, for good things, is then in a special manner as <hi type="italic">precious ointment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.1">Eccl. vii. 1</reference>. Those that honour God he will thus honour, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.3">Ps. cxii. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.6">6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.9">9</reference>. <hi type="italic">The elders</hi> by faith <hi type="italic">obtained a good report</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.2">Heb. xi. 2</reference>), and, being dead, are yet spoken of. 2. It is part of the duty of the survivors: <hi type="italic">Let the memory of the just be blessed,</hi> so the Jews read it, and observe it as a precept, not naming an eminently just man that is dead without adding, <hi type="italic">Let his memory be blessed.</hi> We must delight in making an honourable mention of good men that are gone, bless God for them, and for his gifts and graces that appeared in them, and especially be followers of them in <hi type="italic">that which is good.</hi> <div eID="gen13590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13591" type="x-p"/> II. Bad men are and shall be forgotten, or spoken of with contempt. When their bodies are putrefying in the grave their <hi type="italic">names</hi> also <hi type="italic">shall rot.</hi> Either they shall not be preserved at all, but buried in oblivion (no good can be said of them, and therefore the greatest kindness that can be done them will be to say nothing of them), or they shall be loathsome, and mentioned with detestation, and that rule of honour, <hi type="italic">De mortuis nil nisi bonum</hi>—<hi type="italic">Say nothing to the disadvantage of the dead,</hi> will not protect them. Where the wickedness has been notorious, and cannot but be mentioned, it ought to be mentioned with abhorrence.
entries.8ca2e7e19bdb96bf1b34b17795dfe2ba31c95a5d: <div eID="gen13591" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Marks of Wisdom and of Folly.</title> <div sID="gen13592" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> The wise in heart will receive commandments: but a prating fool shall fall. <div eID="gen13592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13593" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The honour and happiness of the obedient. They <hi type="italic">will receive commandments;</hi> they will take it as a privilege, and really an ease to them, to be under government, which saves them the labour of deliberating and choosing for themselves; and they will take it as a favour to be told their duty and admonished concerning it. And this is their wisdom; those are <hi type="italic">wise in heart</hi> who are tractable, and those who thus bend, thus stoop, shall stand and be established, shall prosper, being well advised. 2. The shame and ruin of the disobedient, that will not be governed, nor endure any yoke, that will not be taught, nor take any advice. They are fools, for they act against themselves and their own interest; they are commonly <hi type="italic">prating fools,</hi> fools of lips, full of talk, but full of nonsense, boasting of themselves, prating spitefully against those that admonish them (<reference osisRef="3John.1.10">3 John 10</reference>), and pretending to give counsel and law to others. Of all fools, none more troublesome than the <hi type="italic">prating fools,</hi> nor that more expose themselves; but they <hi type="italic">shall fall</hi> into sin, into hell, because they received not commandments. Those that are full of tongue seldom look well to their feet, and therefore stumble and fall.
entries.82c4b3a0dadf36a80a767b0de7f4f260f358f9c6: <div eID="gen13593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13594" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> He that walketh uprightly walketh surely: but he that perverteth his ways shall be known. <div eID="gen13594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13595" type="x-p"/> We are here told, and we may depend upon it, 1. That men's integrity will be their security: <hi type="italic">He that walks uprightly</hi> towards God and man, that is faithful to both, that designs as he ought and means as he says, <hi type="italic">walks surely;</hi> he is safe under a divine protection and easy in a holy security. He goes on his way with a humble boldness, being well armed against the temptations of Satan, the troubles of the world, and the reproaches of men. He knows what ground he stands on, what guide he follows, what guard he is surrounded with, and what glory he is going to, and therefore proceeds with assurance and <hi type="italic">great peace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.32.17">Isa. xxxii. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.15-Isa.33.16">xxxiii. 15, 16</reference>. Some understand it as part of the character of an upright man, that he <hi type="italic">walks surely,</hi> in opposition to walking at all adventures. He will not dare to do that which he is not fully satisfied in his own conscience concerning the lawfulness of, but will see his way clear in every thing. 2. That men's dishonesty will be their shame: <hi type="italic">He that perverts his way,</hi> that turns aside into crooked paths, that dissembles with God and man, looks one way and rows another, though he may for a time disguise himself, and pass current, <hi type="italic">shall be known</hi> to be what he is. It is a thousand to one but some time or other he betrays himself; at least, God will discover him in the great day. <hi type="italic">He that perverts his ways documento erit</hi>—<hi type="italic">shall be made an example of,</hi> for warning to others; so some.
entries.91d3d8745067db19da29e47b033dce63fe2b0ff9: <div eID="gen13595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13596" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> He that winketh with the eye causeth sorrow: but a prating fool shall fall. <div eID="gen13596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13597" type="x-p"/> Mischief is here said to attend, 1. Politic, designing, self-disguising sinners: <hi type="italic">He that winks with the eye,</hi> as if he took no notice of you, when at the same time he is watching an opportunity to do you an ill turn, that makes signs to his accomplices when to come into assist him in executing his wicked projects, which are all carried on by trick and artifice, <hi type="italic">causes sorrow</hi> both to others and to himself. Ingenuity will be no excuse for iniquity, but the sinner must either repent or do worse, either rue it or be ruined by it. 2. Public, silly, self-exposing sinners: A <hi type="italic">prating fool,</hi> whose sins go before unto judgment, <hi type="italic">shall fall,</hi> as was said before, <reference osisRef="Prov.10.8">v. 8</reference>. But his case is less dangerous of the two, and, though he destroys himself, he does not create so much sorrow to others as <hi type="italic">he that winks with his eyes.</hi> The dog that bites is not always the dog that barks.
entries.715f749e7ed7da081e6f1d9b5695861c746848a3: <div eID="gen13597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13598" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> The mouth of a righteous <hi type="italic">man is</hi> a well of life: but violence covereth the mouth of the wicked. <div eID="gen13598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13599" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. How industrious a good man is, by communicating his goodness, to do good with it: <hi type="italic">His mouth,</hi> the outlet of his mind, <hi type="italic">is a well of life;</hi> it is a constant spring, whence issues good discourse for the edification of others, like streams that water the ground and make it fruitful, and for their consolation, like streams that quench the thirst of the weary traveller. It is like <hi type="italic">a well of life,</hi> that is pure and clean, not only not poisoned, but not muddled, with any corrupt communication. 2. How industrious a bad man is, by concealing his badness, to do hurt with it: <hi type="italic">The mouth of the wicked covers violence,</hi> disguises the designed mischief with professions of friendship, that it may be carried on the more securely and effectually, as Joab kissed and killed, Judas kissed and betrayed; this is his sin, to which the punishment answers (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Violence covers the mouth of the wicked;</hi> what he got by violence shall by violence be taken from him, <reference osisRef="Job.5.4-Job.5.5">Job v. 4, 5</reference>.
entries.6a1d497df8782482e08c76ed1269b388b6a6763d: <div eID="gen13599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13600" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Hatred stirreth up strifes: but love covereth all sins. <div eID="gen13600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13601" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The great mischief-maker, and that is malice. Even where there is no manifest occasion of strife, yet <hi type="italic">hatred</hi> seeks occasion and so <hi type="italic">stirs it up</hi> and does the devil's work. Those are the most spiteful ill-natured people that can be who take a pleasure in setting their neighbours together by the ears, by tale-bearing, evil surmises, and misrepresentations, blowing up the sparks of contention, which had lain buried, into a flame, at which, with an unaccountable pleasure, they warm their hands. 2. The great peace-maker, and that is <hi type="italic">love,</hi> which <hi type="italic">covers all sins,</hi> that is, the offences among relations which occasion discord. Love, instead of proclaiming and aggravating the offence, conceals and extenuates it as far as it is capable of being concealed and extenuated. Love will excuse the offence which we give through mistake and unadvisedly; when we are able to say that there was no ill intended, but it was an oversight, and we love our friend notwithstanding, this covers it. It will also overlook the offence that is given us, and so cover it, and make the best of it: by this means strife is prevented, or, if begun, peace is recovered and restored quickly. The apostle quotes this, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.8">1 Pet. iv. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">Love will cover a multitude of sins.</hi>
entries.fdf4ff513449e69039a9222e36b412b64e2e6d95: <div eID="gen13601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13602" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> In the lips of him that hath understanding wisdom is found: but a rod <hi type="italic">is</hi> for the back of him that is void of understanding. <div eID="gen13602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13603" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. Wisdom and grace are the honour of good men: He <hi type="italic">that has understanding,</hi> that good understanding which those have that do the commandments, <hi type="italic">wisdom is found in his lips,</hi> that is, it is discovered to be there, and consequently that he has within a good treasure of it, and it is derived thence for the benefit of others. It is a man's honour to have wisdom, but much more to be instrumental to make others wise. 2. Folly and sin are the shame of bad men: <hi type="italic">A rod is for the back of him that is void of understanding—of him that wants a heart;</hi> he exposes himself to the lashes of his own conscience, to the scourges of the tongue, to the censures of the magistrate, and to the righteous judgments of God. Those that foolishly and wilfully go on in wicked ways are preparing rods for themselves, the marks of which will be their perpetual disgrace.
entries.3652e2e58b85edfccb33106404f38e4bf13eb94b: <div eID="gen13603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13604" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> Wise <hi type="italic">men</hi> lay up knowledge: but the mouth of the foolish <hi type="italic">is</hi> near destruction. <div eID="gen13604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13605" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. It is the wisdom of the wise that they treasure up a stock of useful knowledge, which will be their preservation: <hi type="italic">Wisdom is</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">found in their lips</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.13">v. 13</reference>), because it is laid up in their hearts, out of which store, like the good householder, they bring things new and old. Whatever knowledge may be at any time useful to us we must <hi type="italic">lay it up,</hi> because we know not but some time or other we may have occasion for it. We must continue laying up as long as we live; and be sure to lay it up safely, that it may not be to seek when we want it. 2. It is the folly of fools that they lay up mischief in their hearts, which is ready to them in all they say, and works terror and destruction both to others and to themselves. They <hi type="italic">love devouring words</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.52.4">Ps. lii. 4</reference>), and these come uppermost. Their <hi type="italic">mouth is near destruction,</hi> having the <hi type="italic">sharp arrows of bitter words</hi> always at hand to throw about.
entries.30932fc32624ca68cea0e9e2c23615035c75ac7b: <div eID="gen13605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13606" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> The rich man's wealth <hi type="italic">is</hi> his strong city: the destruction of the poor <hi type="italic">is</hi> their poverty. <div eID="gen13606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13607" type="x-p"/> This may be taken two ways:—1. As a reason why we should be diligent in our business, that we may avoid that sinking dispiriting uneasiness which attends poverty, and may enjoy the benefit and comfort which those have that are beforehand in the world. Taking pains is really the way to make ourselves and our families easy. Or, rather, 2. As a representation of the common mistakes both of rich and poor, concerning their outward condition. (1.) Rich people think themselves happy because they are rich; but it is their mistake: <hi type="italic">The rich man's wealth is,</hi> in his own conceit, <hi type="italic">his strong city,</hi> whereas the worst of evils it is too weak and utterly insufficient to protect them from. It will prove that they are not so safe as they imagine; nay, their wealth may perhaps expose them. (2.) Poor people think themselves undone because they are poor; but it is their mistake: <hi type="italic">The destruction of the poor is their poverty;</hi> it sinks their spirits, and ruins all their comforts; whereas a man may live very comfortably, though he has but a little to live on, if he be but content, and keep a good conscience, and live by faith.
entries.f48a3d2980a6686fd577e116e492f3478d52f635: <div eID="gen13607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13608" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> The labour of the righteous <hi type="italic">tendeth</hi> to life: the fruit of the wicked to sin. <div eID="gen13608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13609" type="x-p"/> Solomon here confirms what his father had said (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.16">Ps. xxxvii. 16</reference>), <hi type="italic">A little that a righteous man has is better than the riches of many wicked.</hi> 1. Perhaps a righteous man has no more than what he works hard for; he eats only <hi type="italic">the labour of his hands,</hi> but that <hi type="italic">labour tends to life;</hi> he aims at nothing but to get an honest livelihood, covets not to be rich and great, but is willing to live and maintain his family. Nor does it tend only to his own life, but he would enable himself to do good to others; he labours <hi type="italic">that he may have to give</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.28">Eph. iv. 28</reference>); all his business turns to some good account or other. Or it may be meant of his labour in religion; he takes most pains in that which has a tendency to eternal life; he <hi type="italic">sows to the Spirit,</hi> that he may <hi type="italic">reap life everlasting.</hi> 2. Perhaps a wicked man's wealth is fruit which he did not labour for, but came easily by, but it tends <hi type="italic">to sin.</hi> He makes it the food and fuel of his lusts, his pride and luxury; he gets hurt with it and not good; he gets hurt by it and is hardened by it in his wicked ways. The things of this world are good or evil, life or death, as they are used, and as those are that have them.
entries.a00d2dd4a531525ae8ceae65b854bf0ddf5fd55f: <div eID="gen13609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13610" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> He <hi type="italic">is in</hi> the way of life that keepeth instruction: but he that refuseth reproof erreth. <div eID="gen13610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13611" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. That those are in the right that do not only receive instruction, but retain it, that do not let it slip through carelessness, as most do, nor let it go to those that would rob them of it, that <hi type="italic">keep instruction</hi> safely, keep it pure and entire, keep it for their own use, that they may govern themselves by it, keep it for the benefit of others, that they may instruct them; those that do so are <hi type="italic">in the way of life,</hi> the way that has true comfort in it and eternal life at the end of it. 2. That those are in the wrong that do not only not receive instruction, but wilfully and obstinately refuse it when it is offered them. They will not be taught their duty because it discovers their faults to them; that instruction which carries reproof in it they have a particular aversion to, and certainly they err; it is a sign that they err in judgment, and have false notions of good and evil; it is a cause of their erring in conversation. The traveller that has missed his way, and cannot bear to be told of it and shown the right way, must needs err still, err endlessly; he certainly misses <hi type="italic">the way of life.</hi>
entries.15be503788a1ad06d5c7f06a180b452cb97b577c: <div eID="gen13611" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Proper of the Use of the Tongue.</title> <div sID="gen13612" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> He that hideth hatred <hi type="italic">with</hi> lying lips, and he that uttereth a slander, <hi type="italic">is</hi> a fool. <div eID="gen13612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13613" type="x-p"/> Observe here, Malice is folly and wickedness. 1. It is so when it is concealed by flattery and dissimulation: He <hi type="italic">is a fool,</hi> though he may think himself a politician, <hi type="italic">that hides hatred with lying lips,</hi> lest, if it break out, he should be ashamed before men and should lose the opportunity of gratifying his malice. <hi type="italic">Lying lips</hi> are bad enough of themselves, but have a peculiar malignity in them when they are made <hi type="italic">a cloak of maliciousness.</hi> But he <hi type="italic">is a fool</hi> who thinks to hide any thing from God. 2. It is no better when it is vented in spiteful and mischievous language: <hi type="italic">He that utters slander is a fool</hi> too, for God will sooner or later bring forth that righteousness as the light which he endeavours to cloud, and will find an expedient to roll the reproach away.
entries.3da85be439de1feca38d32403989e9dedffb18e0: <div eID="gen13613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13614" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips <hi type="italic">is</hi> wise. <div eID="gen13614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13615" type="x-p"/> We are here admonished concerning the government of the tongue, that necessary duty of a Christian. 1. It is good to say little, because <hi type="italic">in the multitude of words there wanteth not sin,</hi> or <hi type="italic">sin doth not cease.</hi> Usually, those that speak much speak much amiss, and among many words there cannot but be many idle words, which they must shortly give an account of. Those that love to hear themselves talk do not consider what work they are making for repentance; for that will be wanted, and first or last will be had, where <hi type="italic">there wanteth not sin.</hi> 2. It is therefore good to <hi type="italic">keep our mouth as with a bridle: He that refrains his lips,</hi> that often checks himself, suppresses what he has thought, and holds in that which would transpire, is a wise man; it is an evidence of his wisdom, and he therein consults his own peace. Little said is soon amended, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.13">Amos v. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.1.19">Jam. i. 19</reference>.
entries.afbe0fc462ed86910f98d7c0331192e345f6554a: <div eID="gen13615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13616" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> The tongue of the just <hi type="italic">is as</hi> choice silver: the heart of the wicked <hi type="italic">is</hi> little worth. <hi type="super">21</hi> The lips of the righteous feed many: but fools die for want of wisdom. <div eID="gen13616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13617" type="x-p"/> We are here taught how to value men, not by their wealth and preferment in the world, but by their virtue. <div eID="gen13617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13618" type="x-p"/> I. Good men are good for something. Though they may be poor and low in the world, and may not have power and riches to do good with, yet, as long as they have a mouth to speak, that will make them valuable and useful, and upon that account we must honour those that fear the Lord, because <hi type="italic">out of the good treasure of their heart they bring forth good things.</hi> 1. This makes them valuable: <hi type="italic">The tongue of the just is as choice silver;</hi> they are sincere, freed from the dross of guile and evil design. God's words are compared to <hi type="italic">silver purified</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.12.6">Ps. xii. 6</reference>), for they may be relied on; and such are the words of just men. They are of weight and worth, and will enrich those that hear them with wisdom, which is better than <hi type="italic">choice silver.</hi> 2. It makes them useful: <hi type="italic">The lips of the righteous feed many;</hi> for they are full of the word of God, which is the bread of life, and that sound doctrine wherewith souls are nourished up. Pious discourse is spiritual food to the needy, to the hungry. <div eID="gen13618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13619" type="x-p"/> II. Bad men are good for nothing. 1. One can get no good by them: <hi type="italic">The heart of the wicked is little worth,</hi> and therefore that which comes out of the abundance of his heart cannot be worth much. His principles, his notions, his thoughts, his purposes, and all the things that fill him, and affect him, are worldly and carnal, and therefore of no value. <hi type="italic">He that is of the earth speaks of the earth,</hi> and neither understands nor relishes the things of God, <reference osisRef="John.3.31">John iii. 31</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.14">1 Cor. ii. 14</reference>. The wicked man pretends that, though he does not talk of religion as the just do, yet he has it within him, and thanks God that his heart is good; but he that searches the heart here says the contrary: <hi type="italic">It is nothing worth.</hi> 2. One can do no good to them. While many are fed by <hi type="italic">the lips of the righteous, fools die for want of wisdom;</hi> and fools indeed they are to die for want of that which they might so easily come by. <hi type="italic">Fools die for want of a heart</hi> (so the word is); they perish for want of consideration and resolution; they have no heart to do any thing for their own good. While the righteous feed others fools starve themselves.
entries.faa405bad0fe1ce82501094d022162f651fd6497: <div eID="gen13619" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Advantages of the Righteous.</title> <div sID="gen13620" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> The blessing of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , it maketh rich, and he addeth no sorrow with it. <div eID="gen13620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13621" type="x-p"/> Worldly wealth is that which most men have their hearts very much upon, but they generally mistake both in the nature of the thing they desire and in the way by which they hope to obtain it; we are therefore told here, 1. What that wealth is which is indeed desirable, not having abundance only, but having it and <hi type="italic">no sorrow with it,</hi> no disquieting care to get and keep it, no vexation of spirit in the enjoyment of it, no tormenting grief for the loss of it, no guilt contracted by the abuse of it—to have it and to have a heart to take the comfort of it, to do good with it and to serve God with joyfulness and gladness of heart in the use of it. 2. Whence this desirable wealth is to be expected, not by making ourselves drudges to the world (<reference osisRef="Ps.127.2">Ps. cxxvii. 2</reference>), but by <hi type="italic">the blessing of God.</hi> It is this that <hi type="italic">makes rich and adds no sorrow;</hi> what comes from the love of God has the grace of God for its companion, to preserve the soul from those turbulent lusts and passions of which, otherwise, the increase of riches is commonly the incentive. He had said (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.4">v. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">The hand of the diligent makes rich,</hi> as a means; but here he ascribes it to <hi type="italic">the blessing of the Lord;</hi> but that blessing is upon <hi type="italic">the hand of the diligent.</hi> It is thus in spiritual riches. Diligence in getting them is our duty, but God's blessing and grace must have all the glory of that which is acquired, <reference osisRef="Deut.8.17-Deut.8.18">Deut. viii. 17, 18</reference>.
entries.27125eaeb6d80cff4b13f90d6ec5853e3a77f27b: <div eID="gen13621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13622" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> <hi type="italic">It is</hi> as sport to a fool to do mischief: but a man of understanding hath wisdom. <div eID="gen13622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13623" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. Sin exceedingly sinful: <hi type="italic">It is as laughter to a fool to do mischief;</hi> it is as natural to him, and as pleasant, as it is to a man to laugh. <hi type="italic">Wickedness is his Isaac</hi> (that is the word here); it is his delight, his darling, and that in which he pleases himself. He makes a laughing matter of sin. When he is warned not to sin, from the consideration of the law of God and the revelation of his wrath against sin, he makes a jest of the admonition, and laughs at the shaking of the spear; when he has sinned, instead of sorrowing for it, he boasts of it, ridicules reproofs, and laughs away the convictions of his own conscience, <reference osisRef="Prov.14.9">ch. xiv. 9</reference>. 2. Wisdom exceedingly wise, for it carries along with it the evidence of its own excellency; it may be predicated of itself, and this is encomium enough; you need say no more in praise of <hi type="italic">a man of understanding</hi> than this, "He is an <hi type="italic">understanding man;</hi> he <hi type="italic">has wisdom;</hi> he is so wise as not to do mischief, or if he has, through oversight, offended, he is so wise as not to make a jest of it." Or, to pronounce wisdom wise indeed, read it thus: <hi type="italic">As it is a sport to a fool to do mischief, so it is to a man of understanding to have wisdom and to show it.</hi> Besides the future recompence, a good man has as much present pleasure in the restraints and exercises of religion as sinners can pretend to in the liberties and enjoyments of sin, and much more, and much better.
entries.0b64e34c3b2abf07b999fa07edcb1b91dc770c9a: <div eID="gen13623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13624" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> The fear of the wicked, it shall come upon him: but the desire of the righteous shall be granted. <hi type="super">25</hi> As the whirlwind passeth, so <hi type="italic">is</hi> the wicked no <hi type="italic">more:</hi> but the righteous <hi type="italic">is</hi> an everlasting foundation. <div eID="gen13624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13625" type="x-p"/> It is here said, and said again, to the righteous, that <hi type="italic">it shall be well with them,</hi> and to the wicked, <hi type="italic">Woe to them;</hi> and these are set the one over against the other, for their mutual illustration. <div eID="gen13625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13626" type="x-p"/> I. It shall be as ill with the wicked as they can fear, and as well with the righteous as they can desire. 1. The wicked, it is true, buoy themselves up sometimes in their wickedness with vain hopes which will deceive them, but at other times they cannot but be haunted with just fears, and those <hi type="italic">fears shall come upon them;</hi> the God they provoke will be every whit as terrible as they, when they are under their greatest damps, apprehend him to be. <hi type="italic">As is thy fear, so is thy wrath,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.90.11">Ps. xc. 11</reference>. Wicked men fear the punishment of sin, but they have not wisdom to improve their fears by making their escape, and so the thing they feared comes upon them, and their present terrors are earnests of their future torments. 2. The righteous, it is true, sometimes have their fears, but their desire is towards the favour of God and a happiness in him, and that <hi type="italic">desire shall be granted.</hi> According to their faith, not according to their fear, it shall be <hi type="italic">unto them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.37.4">Ps. xxxvii. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen13626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13627" type="x-p"/> II. The prosperity of the wicked shall quickly end, but the happiness of the righteous shall never end, <reference osisRef="Prov.10.25">v. 25</reference>. The wicked make a great noise, hurry themselves and others, like a <hi type="italic">whirlwind,</hi> which threatens to bear down all before it; but, like a <hi type="italic">whirlwind,</hi> they are presently gone, and they pass irrecoverably; they are <hi type="italic">no more;</hi> all about them are quiet and glad when the storm is over, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.10 Ps.37.36">Ps. xxxvii. 10, 36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.20.5">Job xx. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">The righteous,</hi> on the contrary, make no show; they lie hid, like a <hi type="italic">foundation,</hi> which is low and out of sight, but they are fixed in their resolution to cleave to God, established in virtue, and they shall be an <hi type="italic">everlasting foundation,</hi> immovably good. He that is holy shall be holy still and immovably happy; his hope is built on a rock, and therefore not shocked by the storm, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.24">Matt. vii. 24</reference>. <hi type="italic">The righteous is the pillar of the world</hi> (so some read it); the world stands for their sakes; the holy seed is the substance thereof.
entries.c2709729f02272e70dcbd2c33795f743e2c184a7: <div eID="gen13627" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Righteous Exclusively Happy.</title> <div sID="gen13628" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> As vinegar to the teeth, and as smoke to the eyes, so <hi type="italic">is</hi> the sluggard to them that send him. <div eID="gen13628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13629" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. Those that are of a slothful disposition, that love their ease and cannot apply their minds to any business, are not fit to be employed, no, not so much as to be sent on an errand, for they will neither deliver a message with any care nor make any haste back. Such therefore are very unmeet to be ministers, Christ's messengers; he will not own the sending forth of sluggards into his harvest. 2. Those that are guilty of so great an oversight as to entrust such with any affair, and put confidence in them, will certainly have vexation with them. A slothful servant is to his master as uneasy and troublesome as <hi type="italic">vinegar to the teeth</hi> and <hi type="italic">smoke to the eyes;</hi> he provokes his passion, as vinegar sets the teeth on edge, and occasions him grief to see his business neglected and undone, as smoke sets the eyes a weeping.
entries.ccdcd9656a70d6e03ce6023a94ddcd6da4cdf781: <div eID="gen13629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13630" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> The fear of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> prolongeth days: but the years of the wicked shall be shortened. <hi type="super">28</hi> The hope of the righteous <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> gladness: but the expectation of the wicked shall perish. <div eID="gen13630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13631" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. Religion lengthens men's lives and crowns their hopes. <hi type="italic">What man is he that loves life?</hi> Let him <hi type="italic">fear God,</hi> and that will secure him from many things that would prejudice his life, and secure to him life enough in this world and eternal life in the other; <hi type="italic">the fear of the Lord</hi> will add days more than was expected, will add them endlessly, will prolong them to the days of eternity. <hi type="italic">What man is he that would see good days?</hi> Let him be religious, and then his days shall not only be many, but happy, very happy as well as very many, for <hi type="italic">the hope of the righteous shall be gladness;</hi> they shall have what they hope for, to their unspeakable satisfaction. It is something future and unseen that they place their happiness in (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.24-Rom.8.25">Rom. viii. 24, 25</reference>), not what they have in hand, but what they have in hope, and their hope will shortly be swallowed up in fruition, and it will be their everlasting <hi type="italic">gladness. Enter thou into the joy of thy Lord.</hi> 2. Wickedness shortens men's lives, and frustrates their hopes: <hi type="italic">The years of the wicked,</hi> that are spent in the pleasures of sin and the drudgery of the world, <hi type="italic">shall be shortened.</hi> Cut down the trees that cumber the ground. And whatever comfort or happiness a wicked man promises himself, in this world or the other, he will be frustrated; for <hi type="italic">the expectation of the wicked shall perish;</hi> his hope shall be turned into endless despair.
entries.83e009a0ce6b083f0826fa0a0c2507773ebcbaff: <div eID="gen13631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13632" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">29</hi> The way of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> strength to the upright: but destruction <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> to the workers of iniquity. <hi type="super">30</hi> The righteous shall never be removed: but the wicked shall not inhabit the earth. <div eID="gen13632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13633" type="x-p"/> These two verses are to the same purport with those next before, intimating the happiness of the godly and the misery of the wicked; it is necessary that this be inculcated upon us, so loth are we to believe and consider it. 1. Strength and stability are entailed upon integrity: <hi type="italic">The way of the Lord</hi> (the providence of God, the way in which he walks towards us) <hi type="italic">is strength to the upright,</hi> confirms him in his uprightness. All God's dealings with him, merciful and afflictive, serve to quicken him to his duty and animate him against his discouragements. Or <hi type="italic">the way of the Lord</hi> (the way of godliness, in which he appoints us to walk) is <hi type="italic">strength to the upright;</hi> the closer we keep to that way, the more our hearts are enlarged to proceed in it, the better fitted we are both for services and sufferings. A good conscience, kept pure from sin, gives a man boldness in a dangerous time, and constant diligence in duty makes a man's work easy in a busy time. The more we do for God the more we may do, <reference osisRef="Job.17.9">Job xvii. 9</reference>. That <hi type="italic">joy of the Lord</hi> which is to be found only in the <hi type="italic">way of the Lord</hi> will be our strength (<reference osisRef="Neh.8.10">Neh. viii. 10</reference>), and therefore <hi type="italic">the righteous shall never be removed.</hi> Those that have an established virtue have an established peace and happiness which nothing can rob them of; they <hi type="italic">have an everlasting foundation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.10.25">v. 25</reference>. 2. Ruin and destruction are the certain consequences of wickedness. <hi type="italic">The wicked shall not</hi> only not inherit the earth, though they lay up their treasure in it, but they shall not so much as <hi type="italic">inhabit the earth;</hi> God's judgments will root them out. <hi type="italic">Destruction,</hi> swift and sure destruction, <hi type="italic">shall be to the workers of iniquity,</hi> destruction from the presence of the Lord and the glory of his power. Nay, that way of the Lord which is the strength of the upright is consumption and terror <hi type="italic">to the workers of iniquity;</hi> the same gospel which to the one is a <hi type="italic">savour of life unto life</hi> to the other is a <hi type="italic">savour of death unto death;</hi> the same providence, like the same sun, softens the one and hardens the other, <reference osisRef="Hos.14.9">Hos. xiv. 9</reference>.
entries.70b00c2dd4c403df9c48b78ca656fa4847fba874: <div eID="gen13633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13634" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> The mouth of the just bringeth forth wisdom: but the froward tongue shall be cut out. <hi type="super">32</hi> The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable: but the mouth of the wicked <hi type="italic">speaketh</hi> frowardness. <div eID="gen13634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13635" type="x-p"/> Here, as before, men are judged of, and, accordingly, are justified or condemned, by their words, <reference osisRef="Matt.12.37">Matt. xii. 37</reference>. 1. It is both the proof and the praise of a man's wisdom and goodness that he speaks wisely and well. A good man, in his discourse, <hi type="italic">brings forth wisdom</hi> for the benefit of others. God gives him wisdom as a reward of his righteousness (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.26">Eccl. ii. 26</reference>), and he, in gratitude for that gift and justice to the giver, does good with it, and with his wise and pious discourses edifies many. He <hi type="italic">knows what is acceptable,</hi> what discourse will be pleasing to God (for that is it that he studies more than to oblige the company), and what will be agreeable both to the speaker and to the hearers, what will become him and benefit them, and that he will speak. 2. It is the sin, and will be the ruin, of a wicked man, that he speaks wickedly like himself. <hi type="italic">The mouth of the wicked speaks frowardness,</hi> that which is displeasing to God and provoking to those he converses with; and what is the issue of it? Why, <hi type="italic">the froward tongue shall be cut out,</hi> as surely as the <hi type="italic">flattering one,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.12.3">Ps. xii. 3</reference>.  <chapter eID="Prov.10"/> <div eID="gen13635" type="x-p"/>

entries.6a0dad78f3f9d6062b3ff0713e05372caa6f9122: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7371"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 10</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Prov.10.1-Prov.10.32">Pr 10:1-32</reference>. Here begins the second part of the book, Pr 10:1-22:16, which, with the third, Pr 22:16-25:28, contains series of proverbs whose sense is complete in one or two verses, and which, having no logical connection, admit of no analysis. The parallelisms of Pr 10:<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.33">1-15:33</reference> are mostly antithetic; and those of Pr 16:1-22:16, synthetic. The evidences of art in the structure are very clear, and indicate, probably, a purpose of facilitating the labor of memorizing.</title> <div sID="gen11383" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7371"/><hi type="bold">1. wise [and] foolish--</hi>as they follow or reject the precepts of wisdom.<div eID="gen11383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11384" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">maketh ... father--</hi>or, "gladdens a father."<div eID="gen11384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11385" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heaviness--</hi>or, "grief." <div eID="gen11385" type="x-p"/>
entries.24808b90f4b2ba127a38eb7328ef7722681bd3bb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7372"/><div sID="gen11386" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7372"/><hi type="bold">2. Treasures ... nothing--</hi>that is, Ill-gotten gains give no true happiness (compare <reference osisRef="Prov.4.17">Pr 4:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.6.19">Mt 6:19</reference>).<div eID="gen11386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11387" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">righteousness--</hi>especially beneficence (<reference osisRef="Ps.112.9">Psa 112:9</reference>).<div eID="gen11387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11388" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">death--</hi>the greatest of all evils. <div eID="gen11388" type="x-p"/>
entries.eb2a380a5da8afab9b42ff75c2a188795b20e769: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7373"/><div sID="gen11389" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7373"/>3. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.37.16-Ps.37.20">Psa 37:16-20</reference>). The last clause is better: "He will repel the greedy desires of the wicked." <div eID="gen11389" type="x-p"/>

entries.a914124a427668a1e55a69d349f776e675be647a: <div eID="gen24080" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen24081" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24082" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24082" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24081" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24083" type="x-p"/> It is impossible to give summaries of such chapters as these, where almost every verse contains a separate subject. Our common version not being able to exhibit the contents as usual, simply says, "From this chapter to the five and twentieth are sundry observations upon moral virtues, and their opposite vices." In general the wise man states in this chapter the difference between the wise and the foolish, the righteous and the wicked, the diligent and the idle. He speaks also of love and hatred, of the good and the evil tongue, or of the slanderer and the peace-maker. <div eID="gen24083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24084" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen24084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24085" type="x-p"/> The proverbs of Solomon - Some ancient MSS. of the Vulgate have Proverbiorum liber secundus, "The second book of the Proverbs." The preceding nine chapters can only be considered as an introduction, if indeed they may be said to make even a part, of the proverbs of Solomon, which appear to commence only at the tenth chapter. <div eID="gen24085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24086" type="x-p"/> A wise son maketh a glad father - The parallels in this and several of the succeeding chapters are those which Bishop Lowth calls the antithetic; when two lines correspond with each other by an opposition of terms and sentiments; when the second is contrasted with the first; sometimes in expression, sometimes in sense only. Accordingly the degrees of antithesis are various; from an exact contraposition of word to word, through a whole sentence, down to a general disparity, with something of a contrariety in the two propositions, as: - <div eID="gen24086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24087" type="x-p"/> A wise son rejoiceth in his father. <div eID="gen24087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24088" type="x-p"/> But a foolish son is the grief of his mother. <div eID="gen24088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24089" type="x-p"/> Where every word has its opposite; for the terms father and mother are, as the logicians say, relatively opposite.
entries.206518c0a09554e57d7de6d252a18338ef4f3afb: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen24089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24090" type="x-p"/> Treasures of wickedness - Property gained by wicked means. <div eID="gen24090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24091" type="x-p"/> Delivered from death - Treasures gained by robbery often bring their possessors to an untimely death; but those gained by righteous dealing bring with them no such consequences.
entries.d7391713d9c78419b14aff54cb55427265bee686: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen24091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24092" type="x-p"/> But he casteth away the substance of the wicked - But instead of רשעים reshaim, the wicked, בוגדים bogedim, hypocrites, or perfidious persons, is the reading of twelve or fourteen of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS., and some editions; but it is not acknowledged by any of the ancient versions. <div eID="gen24092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24093" type="x-p"/> The righteous have God for their feeder; and because of his infinite bounty, they can never famish for want of the bread of life. On the contrary, the wicked are often, in the course of his providence, deprived of the property of which they make a bad use.
entries.c07aa9057d8112887f5660d6ddc259c585c88611: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen24093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24094" type="x-p"/> He becometh poor - God has ordered, in the course of his providence, that he who will not work shall not eat. And he always blesses the work of the industrious man.
entries.66347b37e419a96e6a59ef14a94fb767486d68e6: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen24094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24095" type="x-p"/> He that gathereth in summer - All the work of the field should be done in the season suitable to it. If summer and harvest be neglected, in vain does a man expect the fruits of autumn.
entries.c07b70facc37edd25605926a335502339a2d1b8d: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen24095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24096" type="x-p"/> Violence covereth the mouth of the wicked - As blessings shall be on the head of the just, so the violence of the wicked shall cover their face with shame and confusion. Their own violent dealings shall be visited upon them. The mouth forsoth of unpitious men wickidnesse covereth. - Old MS. Bible. "The forehead of the ungodly is past shame, and presumptuous." - Coverdale.
entries.44711bfc05c552055adc5d6fc2cce4ae0d26dfef: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen24096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24097" type="x-p"/> The memory of the just is blessed - Or, is a blessing. <div eID="gen24097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24098" type="x-p"/> But the name of the wicked shall rot - This is another antithesis; but there are only two antithetic terms, for memory and name are synonymous - Lowth. The very name of the wicked is as offensive as putrid carrion.
entries.6d3016c192bd833d354644ad299567d949ce5322: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen24098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24099" type="x-p"/> A prating fool shall fall - This clause is repeated in the tenth verse. The wise man will receive the commandment: but the shallow blabbing fool shall be cast down. See <reference osisRef="Pro.10.10">Pro 10:10</reference>.
entries.7333f5af5d49a8a25d04d74ff408015232fc3cc6: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen24099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24100" type="x-p"/> He that walketh uprightly - The upright man is always safe; he has not two characters to support; he goes straight forward, and is never afraid of detection, because he has never been influenced by hypocrisy or deceit.
entries.898d9963043332125f7705a5ff90b2501703c48e: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen24100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24101" type="x-p"/> He that winketh with the eye - Instead of the latter clause, on which see <reference osisRef="Pro.10.8">Pro 10:8</reference>, the Septuagint has, ὁ δε ελεγχων μετα παῥρησιας ειρηνοποιει· "but he that reproveth with freedom, maketh peace." This is also the reading of the Syriac and Arabic. A faithful open reproving of sin is more likely to promote the peace of society than the passing it by slightly, or taking no notice of it; for if the wicked turn to God at the reproof, the law of peace will soon be established in his heart, and the law of kindness will flow from his tongue.
entries.45377cfb24e0a26bc8315bc01c7a585136e7d1cf: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen24101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24102" type="x-p"/> The mouth of a righteous man is a well of life - מקור חיים mekor chaiyim, is the vein of lives; an allusion to the great aorta, which conveys the blood from the heart to every art of the body. The latter clause of this verse is the same with that of <reference osisRef="Pro.10.6">Pro 10:6</reference>.
entries.8c979d641e82da7430a8eaddcd4fbcfed519f5d1: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen24102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24103" type="x-p"/> Hatred stirreth up strifes - It seeks for occasions to provoke enmity. It delights in broils. On the contrary, love conciliates; removes aggravations; puts the best construction on every thing; and pours water, not oil, upon the flame.
entries.c0c391be115d6e6f7caa8fece9eb574f34914a83: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen24103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24104" type="x-p"/> A rod is for the back of him - He that can learn, and will not learn, should be made to learn. The rod is a most powerful instrument of knowledge. Judiciously applied, there is a lesson of profound wisdom in every twig.
entries.4fdd1ae817eeb3944ec8f8f6b155f1fb8a5a7fdb: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen24104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24105" type="x-p"/> Wise men lay up knowledge - They keep secret every thing that has a tendency to disturb domestic or public peace; but the foolish man blabs all out, and produces much mischief. Think much, speak little, and always think before you speak. This will promote your own peace and that of your neighbor.
entries.6d968e350e49485ee9702f04bb0b835f2ce37649: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen24105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24106" type="x-p"/> The rich man's wealth is his strong city - Behold a mystery in providence; there is not a rich man on earth but becomes such by means of the poor! Property comes from the labor of the poor, and the king himself is served of the field. How unjust, diabolically so, is it to despise or oppress those by whose labor all property is acquired! <div eID="gen24106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24107" type="x-p"/> The destruction of the poor is their poverty - A man in abject poverty never arises out of this pit. They have no nucleus about which property may aggregate. The poet spoke well: - <div eID="gen24107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24108" type="x-p"/> Haud facile emergunt, quorum virtutibus obstat <div eID="gen24108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24109" type="x-p"/> Res angusta domi. "They rarely emerge from poverty, whose exertions are cramped by want at home."
entries.c5eeebeae62c24e3516b77b937340f7562a8e910: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen24109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24110" type="x-p"/> The labor of the righteous - The good man labors that he may be able to support life; this is his first object: and then to have something to divide with the poor; this is his next object. <div eID="gen24110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24111" type="x-p"/> The fruit of the wicked to sin - This man lives to eat and drink, and his property he spends in riot and excess. God's blessings are cursed to him.
entries.e85f1349f0b346583d17d94b9182b59f554da7ad: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen24111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24112" type="x-p"/> He is in the way of life - The truly religious man accumulates knowledge that he may the better know how to live to God, and do most good among men.
entries.5e1214f8deac8a9e72d2487884d213bd2fc3b963: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen24112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24113" type="x-p"/> He that hideth - This is a common case. How many, when full of resentment, and deadly hatred, meditating revenge and cruelty, and sometimes even murder, have pretended that they thought nothing of the injury they had sustained; had passed by the insult, etc.! Thus lying lips covered the malevolence of a wicked heart.
entries.ca6bd65092de75e82ef97a68d9cfc532bc0f8d82: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen24113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24114" type="x-p"/> In the multitude of words - It is impossible to speak much, and yet speak nothing but truth; and injure no man's character in the mean while.
entries.2a4dda7174790da06377e80ede3bf63f8256a3a8: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen24114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24115" type="x-p"/> The heart of the wicked is little worth - כמעט kimat, is like little or nothing; or is like dross, while the tongue of the just is like silver. A sinner's heart is worth nothing, and is good for nothing; and yet because it is his most hidden part, he vaunts of its honesty, goodness, etc.! Yes, yes; it is very honest and good, only the devil is in it! that is all.
entries.d3a4268adbcb9f03660b24ae4ea0f2008e30f168: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen24115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24116" type="x-p"/> The blessing of the Lord, it maketh rich - Whatever we receive in the way of providence, has God's blessing in it, and will do us good. Cares, troubles, and difficulties come with all property not acquired in this way; but God's blessing gives simple enjoyment, and levies no tax upon the comfort.
entries.62a0072e67c2241cb1ff1466c94da0defb083511: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen24116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24117" type="x-p"/> It is a sport to a fool to do mischief - What a millstone weight of iniquity hangs about the necks of most of the jesters. facetious and witty people! "How many lies do they tell in jest, to go to the devil in earnest!"
entries.830c21754b39c090c9d16128c575ef6b611fbd2d: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen24117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24118" type="x-p"/> The fear of the wicked - The wicked is full of fears and alarms; and all that he has dreaded and more than he has dreaded, shall come upon him. The righteous is always desiring more of the salvation of God, and God will exceed even his utmost desires.
entries.daef74cfc012102a309fa2eccdc8c57273f6a93c: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen24118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24119" type="x-p"/> As the whirlwind passeth - As tornadoes that sweep every thing away before them; so shall the wrath of God sweep away the wicked; it shall leave him neither branch nor root. But the righteous, being built on the eternal foundation, יסוד עולם yesod olam, shall never be shaken.
entries.24bf0aeb063eee39d08e85979c8d17089f7a1986: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen24119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24120" type="x-p"/> As vinegar to the teeth - The acid softening and dissolving the alkali of the bone, so as to impair their texture, and render them incapable of masticating; and as smoke affects the eyes, irritating their tender vessels, so as to give pain and prevent distinct vision; so the sluggard, the lounging, thriftless messenger, who never returns in time with the desired answer.
entries.217759ae71d796cfbe6d77811c567436b889828d: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen24120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24121" type="x-p"/> The expectation of the wicked shall perish - A wicked man is always imposing on himself by the hope of God's mercy and final happiness; and he continues hoping, till he dies without receiving that mercy which alone would entitle him to that glory.
entries.ab27d2b9c662fa3ea5d6255d3cc1f3f80f5c3794: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen24121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24122" type="x-p"/> The way of the Lord is strength - In the path of obedience the upright man ever finds his strength renewed; the more he labors the stronger he grows. The same sentiment as that in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.31">Isa 40:31</reference>.
entries.cddd77a9d4989727927897a4e3f2b41d1d85f6e6: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen24122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24123" type="x-p"/> The righteous shall never be removed - Because he is built on the eternal foundation. See on <reference osisRef="Pro.10.25">Pro 10:25</reference> (note).
entries.88c4e21c311ed31f0ecf3f172dce4e57bb1721d8: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen24123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24124" type="x-p"/> The froward tongue shall be cut out - This probably alludes to the punishment of cutting out the tongue for blasphemy, treasonable speeches, profane swearing, or such like. The tunge of schrewis schal perishen. - Old MS. Bible. Were the tongue of every shrew or scold to be extracted, we should soon have much less noise in the world.
entries.09d98f1d3f080d3c2c52e935e6a0fc7b3287dad4: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen24124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24125" type="x-p"/> The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable - And what they believe to be most pleasing and most profitable, that they speak, but the wicked man knows as well what is perverse, and that he speaketh forth. As the love of God is not in his heart, so the law of kindness is not on his lips.  <chapter eID="Prov.10"/> <div eID="gen24125" type="x-p"/>

entries.408fd1f0e2ff4dc7a06703fac5e82472040e4c48: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.1">Pro 10:1</reference> <div eID="gen10871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10872" type="x-p"/> In the introduction, chap. 1-9, there are larger sections of interconnected thoughts having one common aim. Even in <reference osisRef="Prov.6.1-Prov.6.19">Prov 6:1-19</reference> there are manifestly three proverbial discourses distinguished from one another, shorter indeed, yet containing one fundamental thought. Such proverbs as are primarily designed to form one completed little whole of themselves, are not here to be met with. On the contrary, the Solomonic collection which now follows consists of pure distichs, for the most part antithetical, but at the same time going over all the forms of the technical proverb, as we have already shown; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., p. 16. Accordingly the exposition must from this point onward renounce reproduced combinations of thought. The succession of proverbs here is nevertheless not one that is purely accidental or without thought; it is more than a happy accident when three of the same character stand together; the collector has connected together proverb with proverb according to certain common characteristics (Bertheau). And yet more than that: the mass separates itself into groups, not merely succeeding one another, but because a certain connection of ideas connects together a number of proverbs, in such a way that the succession is broken, and a new point of departure is arrived at (Hitzig). There is no comprehensive plan, such as Oetinger in his summary view of its contents supposes; the progressive unfolding follows no systematic scheme, but continuously wells forth. But that the editor, whom we take also to be the arranger of the contents of the book, did not throw them together by good chance, but in placing them together was guided by certain reasons, the very first proverb here shows, for it is chosen in conformity with the design of this book, which is specially dedicated to youth: 1 A wise son maketh glad his father;    A foolish son is his mother’s grief. <div eID="gen10872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10873" type="x-p"/> One sees here quite distinctly (cf. Hos 13:13) that חכם (from חכם, properly to be thick, stout, solid, as πυκνός = σοφός) is primarily a practical and ethical conception. Similar proverbs are found further on, but consisting of synonymous parallel members, in which either the father both times represents the parents, as <reference osisRef="Prov.17.21">Pro 17:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.23.24">Pro 23:24</reference>, or father and mother are separated, each being named in different members, as <reference osisRef="Prov.17.25">Pro 17:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.23.25">Pro 23:25</reference>, and particularly <reference osisRef="Prov.15.20">Pro 15:20</reference>, where 20a = 1a of the above proverb. It is incorrect to say, with Hitzig, that this contrast draws the division after it: the division lies nearer in the synonymous distichs, and is there less liable to be misunderstood than in the antithetic. Thus, from this proverb before us, it might be concluded that grief on account of a befooled son going astray in bypaths, and not coming to the right way, falls principally on the mother, as (Sir. 3:9) is often the case in unfortunate marriages. The idea of the parents is in this way only separated, and the two members stand in suppletive interchangeable relationship. ישׂמּח is the middle of the clause, and is the usual form in connection; ישׂמּח is the pausal form. תּוּגה, from הוגה (יגה), has <hi type="italic">pass. û</hi>, as תּורה, <hi type="italic">act. ô</hi>. “The expression of the <hi type="italic">pred</hi>. 1b is like <reference osisRef="Prov.3.17">Pro 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.8.6">Pro 8:6</reference>; Pro 10:14.; cf. <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Arab. âlastaḳṣa furkat, oversharpening is dividing, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, effects it inquiries become or lead to separation (cf. our proverb, <hi type="italic">Allzuscharf macht scharig</hi> = too much sharpening makes full of notches); Burckhardt, Sprüchw. Nr. 337” (Fl.).
entries.e4c6d3752d688337f6296ebf07054fb4538176d4: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.2">Pro 10:2</reference> <div eID="gen10873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10874" type="x-p"/> There follows now a series of proverbs which place possessions and goods under a moral-religious point of view: <div eID="gen10874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10875" type="x-p"/> Treasures of wickedness bring no profit; <div eID="gen10875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10876" type="x-p"/> But righteousness delivers from death. <div eID="gen10876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10877" type="x-p"/> The lxx and Aquila translate ἀνόμους (ἀσεβεῖς). הועיל (to profit) with the accus. is possible, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.12">Isa 57:12</reference>, but אוצרות one does not use by itself; it requires a genitive designating it more closely. But also דּרשּׂיעא of the Targ., παρανόμων of Symmachus, fails; for the question still remains, to whom? Rightly Syr., Jerome, Theodotion, and the Quinta: ἀσεβείας, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.4.17">Pro 4:17</reference>; Mic 4:10; <reference osisRef="Luke.16.9">Luk 16:9</reference>, μαμωνᾶς τῆς ἀδικίας. Treasures to which wickedness cleaves profit not, viz., him who has collected them through wickedness. On the contrary, righteousness saves from death (2b = <reference osisRef="Prov.11.4">Pro 11:4</reference>, where the parallelism makes it clear that death as a judgment is meant). In <reference osisRef="Deut.24.13">Deu 24:13</reference> it had been already said that compassionate love is “righteousness before the Lord,” the cardinal virtue of the righteousness of life. Faith (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.4">Hab 2:4</reference>) is its soul, and love its life. Therefore δικαιοσύνη and ἐεημοσύνη are interchangeable ideas; and it ought not to be an objection against the Apocrypha that it repeats the above proverb, ἐλεημοσύνη ἐκ θανάτου ῥύεται, Tob. 4:10; 12:9, Sir. 3:30; 29:12, for <reference osisRef="Dan.4.24">Dan 4:24</reference> also says the very same thing, and the thought is biblical, in so far as the giving of alms is understood to be not a dead work, but (<reference osisRef="Ps.112.9">Psa 112:9</reference>) the life-activity of one who fears God, and of a mind believing in Him and resting in His word.
entries.417b5c69311e1035495c59659bca38187fe89943: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.3">Pro 10:3</reference> <div eID="gen10877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10878" type="x-p"/> Another proverb, the members of which stand in chiastic relation to those of the preceding: <div eID="gen10878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10879" type="x-p"/> Jahve does not suffer the soul of the righteous to hunger; <div eID="gen10879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10880" type="x-p"/> But the craving of the godless He disappointeth. <div eID="gen10880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10881" type="x-p"/> The thought is the same as Pro 13:25. There, as also at <reference osisRef="Prov.6.30">Pro 6:30</reference>, the soul is spoken of as the faculty of desire, and that after nourishment, for the lowest form of the life of the soul is the impulse to self-preservation. The parallel הוּה, in which lxx and Ar. erroneously find the meaning of חיּה, life, the Syr. Targ. the meaning of הון, possession, means the desire, without however being related to אוּה (Berth.); it is the Arab. hawan, from הוה, Arab. haway, which, from the fundamental meaning χαίνειν, <hi type="italic">hiare</hi>, to gape, yawn, signifies not only unrestrained driving along, and crashing overthrow (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.11.6">Pro 11:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.19.13">Pro 19:13</reference>), but also the breaking forth, <hi type="italic">ferri in aliquid</hi>, whence הוּה, Arab. hawan, violent desire, in Hebr. generally (here and <reference osisRef="Ps.52.9">Psa 52:9</reference>, Mich. <reference osisRef="Prov.7.3">Pro 7:3</reference>) of desire without limits and without restraint (cf. the plur. âhawâ, arbitrary actions, caprices); the meanings deduced from this important verbal stem (of which also הוה היה, <hi type="italic">accidere</hi>, and then <hi type="italic">esse</hi>, at least after the Arabic conception of speech, is an offshoot) are given by Fleischer under <reference osisRef="Job.37.6">Job 37:6</reference>, and after Fleischer by Ethé, <hi type="italic">Schlafgemach der Phantasie</hi>, ii. p. 6f. The verb הדף signifies to push in the most manifold shades, here to push forth, <hi type="italic">repellere</hi>, as 2Ki 4:27 (cf. Arab. ḥadhaf, to push off = to discharge); the fut. is invariably יהדּף, like יהגּה. God gives satisfaction to the soul of the righteous, viz., in granting blessings. The desire of the wicked He does not suffer to be accomplished; it may appear for a long time as if that which was aimed at was realized, but in the end God pushes it back, so that it remains at a distance, because contrary to Him. Instead of והות רשׁעים, some editions (Plantin 1566, Bragadin 1615) have והות בּגדים, but, in opposition to all decided testimony, only through a mistaken reference to Pro 11:6.
entries.81c86fb7aad4531f6d0331b567de5b1b61230da0: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.4">Pro 10:4</reference> <div eID="gen10881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10882" type="x-p"/> There follow two proverbs which say how one man fails and another succeeds: <div eID="gen10882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10883" type="x-p"/> He becomes poor who bears a sluggish hand; <div eID="gen10883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10884" type="x-p"/> But the hand of the diligent maketh rich. <div eID="gen10884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10885" type="x-p"/> These three proverbs, <reference osisRef="Prov.19.15">Pro 19:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.12.24">Pro 12:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.12.27">Pro 12:27</reference>, are similar. From the last two it is seen that רמיּה is a subst., as also from Psa 120:2. (לשׁון רמיּה, from a crafty tongue) that it is an adject., and from Lev 14:15. (where כּף is fem.) that it may be at the same time an adject. here also. The masc. is רמי, like טרי to טריּה ot , but neither of these occur; “the fundamental idea is that of throwing oneself down lazily, when one with unbent muscles holds himself no longer erect and stretched, Arab. taramy” (Fl.). The translation: deceitful balances (Löwenstein after Rashi), is contrary to biblical usage, which knows nothing of כף in this Mishnic meaning. But if כף is here regarded as fem., then it cannot be the subject (Jerome, <hi type="italic">egestatem operata est manus remissa</hi>), since we read עשׂה, not עשׂה. But ראשׁ also is not suitable as the subject (lxx, Syr., Targ.), for poverty is called רישׁ, רישׁ, ראשׁ; on the contrary, רשׁ, plur. רשׁים or ראשׁים, is used adjectively. Since now the adject. רשׁ, <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.14">1Sa 12:14</reference>, is also written ראשׁ, it may be translated: Poor is he who... (Bertheau); but we much rather expect the statement of that which happens to such an one, thus: Poor will he be... ראשׁ, 3 <hi type="italic">praet</hi>. = רשׁ, <reference osisRef="Ps.34.11">Psa 34:11</reference>, with the same (grammatically incorrect) full writing as קאם, Hos 10:14. In the conception of the subject, כף־רמיה, after <reference osisRef="Jer.48.10">Jer 48:10</reference>, is interpreted as the accus. of the manner (Berth.: whoever works with sluggish hand); but since עשׂה רמיה (in another sense indeed: to practise cunning) is a common phrase, <reference osisRef="Ps.52.4">Psa 52:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.101.7">Psa 101:7</reference>, so also will כף־רמיה be regarded as the object: <hi type="italic">qui agit manum remissam</hi>, whoever carries or moves such a hand (Hitzig).
