In 4b working is placed opposite to bearing: the diligent hand makes rich, <hi type="italic">ditat</hi> or <hi type="italic">divitias parit</hi>; but not for itself (Gesen. and others: becomes rich), but for him who bears it. The diligent man is called חרוּץ, from חרץ, to sharpen, for, as in ὀξύς, <hi type="italic">acer</hi>, sharpness is transferred to energy; the form is the same as הלּוּק, smooth (for the ā is unchangeable, because recompensative), a kindred form to קטול like חמוץ, and Arab. fâ'ûl as fashawsh, a boaster, wind-bag, either of active (as חנּוּן) or (as חלוק, חרוץ, עמּוּד, שׁכּוּל) of passive signification.
entries.e56cfb97cd29ff3df8b0139611199623ccb17b84: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.5">Pro 10:5</reference> <div eID="gen10885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10886" type="x-p"/> There is now added a proverb which, thus standing at the beginning of the collection, and connecting itself with <reference osisRef="Prov.10.1">Pro 10:1</reference>, stamps on it the character of a book for youth: <div eID="gen10886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10887" type="x-p"/> He that gathereth in summer is a wise son; <div eID="gen10887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10888" type="x-p"/> But he that is sunk in sleep in the time of harvest is a son that causeth shame. <div eID="gen10888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10889" type="x-p"/> Von Hofmann (Schriftb. ii. 2. 403) rightly interprets בּן משׂכּיל and בּן מבישׁ, with Cocceius and others, as the subject, and not with Hitzig as predicate, for in nominal clauses the rule is to place the predicate before the subject; and since an accurate expression of the inverted relation would both times require הוא referring to the subject, so we here abide by the usual syntax: he that gathers in summer time is... Also the relation of the members of the sentence, <reference osisRef="Prov.19.26">Pro 19:26</reference>, is a parallel from which it is evident that the misguided son is called מבישׁ as causing shame, although in הבישׁ the idea to put to shame (= to act so that others are ashamed) and to act shamefully (disgracefully), as in השׂכיל the ideas to have insight and to act intelligently, lie into one another (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.14.35">Pro 14:35</reference>); the root-meaning of השׂכיל is determined after שׂכל, which from שׂכל, <hi type="italic">complicare</hi>, designates the intellect as the faculty of intellectual configuration. בּושׁ, properly <hi type="italic">disturbari</hi>, proceeds from a similar conception as the Lat. <hi type="italic">confundi</hi> (<hi type="italic">pudore</hi>). קיץ and קציר fall together, for קיץ (from קוץ = qât, to be glowing hot) is just the time of the קציר; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under Gen 8:22. To the activity of a thoughtful ingathering, אגר, for a future store (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.6.7">Pro 6:7</reference>), stands opposed deep sleep, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the state of one sunk in idleness. נרדּם means, as Schultens has already shown, <hi type="italic">somno penitus obrui, omni sensu obstructo et oppilato quasi</hi>, from רדם, to fill, to shut up, to conclude; the derivation (which has been adopted since Gesenius) from the Arab. word having the same sound, rdm, <hi type="italic">stridere</hi>, to shrill, to rattle (but not <hi type="italic">stertere</hi>, to snore), lies remote in the <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>., and also contradicts the usage of the word, according to which it designates a state in which all free activity is bound, and all reference to the external world is interrupted; cf. תּרדּמה, <reference osisRef="Prov.19.15">Pro 19:15</reference>, of dulness, apathy, somnolency in the train of slothfulness. The lxx has here one distich more than the Hebr. text.
entries.9029177ffab1ab1e0de7118961d12e4a24f5704c: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.6">Pro 10:6</reference> <div eID="gen10889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10890" type="x-p"/> There now follow two proverbs regarding the blessings and the curses which come to men, and which flow forth from them. Here, however, as throughout, we take each proverb by itself, that it might not appear as if we had a tetrastich before us. The first of these two antithetic distichs is: <div eID="gen10890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10891" type="x-p"/> Blessings (come) on the head of the just; <div eID="gen10891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10892" type="x-p"/> But violence covereth the mouth of the godless. <div eID="gen10892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10893" type="x-p"/> Blessings are, without being distinguished, bestowed as well as prayed for from above. Regarding the undistinguished uses of לראשׁ (of a recompense of reward), בּראשׁ (of penal recompense), and על־ראשׁ (especially of punishment), <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under Gen 49:26. If we understand, with Ewald, Bertheau, Elster, Zöckler, and others, the two lines after <reference osisRef="Prov.10.11">Pro 10:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.19.28">Pro 19:28</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.10.18">Pro 10:18</reference> : the mouth of the wicked covers (hides under a mask) violence, inasmuch as he speaks words of blessing while thoughts of malediction lurk behind them (<reference osisRef="Ps.62.5">Psa 62:5</reference>), then we renounce the sharpness of the contrast. On the contrary, it is preserved if we interpret וּפי as object: the violence that has gone out from it covereth the mouth of the wicked, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, it falls back upon his foul mouth; or as Fleischer (and Oetinger almost the same) paraphrases it: the deeds of violence that have gone forth from them are given back to them in curses and maledictions, so that going back they stop, as it were, their mouth, they bring them to silence; for it is unnecessary to take פי synecdochically for פני (cf. <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.8">Psa 69:8</reference>), since in בּרכות 6a are perhaps chiefly meant blessings of thankful acknowledgment on the part of men, and the giving prominence to the mouth of the wicked from which nothing good proceeds is well accounted for. The parallels do not hinder us thus to explain, since parts of proverbs repeating themselves in the Book of Proverbs often show a change of the meaning (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., p. 24f.). Hitzig’s conjecture, יכּסה (better יכסּה), is unnecessary; for elsewhere we read, as here, that חמס (violence), <hi type="italic">jure talionis</hi>, covers, יכּסּה, the wicked, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.17">Hab 2:17</reference>, or that he, using “violence,” therewith covers the whole of his external appearance, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, gives to it the branded impress of the unrighteousness he has done (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Köhler under Mal 2:16).
entries.2952171fa91321db33dde3d6a870c6196a78724b: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.7">Pro 10:7</reference> <div eID="gen10893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10894" type="x-p"/> Thus, as <reference osisRef="Prov.10.6">Pro 10:6</reference> says how it goes with the righteous and the wicked in this life, so this verse tells how it fares with them after death: <div eID="gen10894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10895" type="x-p"/> The memory of the righteous remains in blessings, <div eID="gen10895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10896" type="x-p"/> And the name of the godless rots. <div eID="gen10896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10897" type="x-p"/> The tradition regarding the writing of זכר with five (זכר) or six points (זכר) is doubtful (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Heidenheim in his ed. of the Pentateuch, <hi type="italic">Meôr Enajim</hi>, under <reference osisRef="Exod.17.14">Exo 17:14</reference>); the Cod. 1294 and old printed copies have here זכר. Instead of לברכה, יברך might be used; the phrase היה לברכה (opp. היה לקללה, often used by Jeremiah), subordinate to the substantival clause, paraphrases the passive, for it expresses a growing to something, and thus the entrance into a state of endurance. The remembrance of the righteous endures after his death, for he is thought of with thankfulness (צל''ז = זכר צדיק לברכה, the usual appendix to the name of an honoured, beloved man who has died), because his works, rich in blessing, continue; the name of the godless, on the contrary, far from continuing fresh and green (Psa 62:1-12 :17) after his departure, becomes corrupt (רקב, from רק, to be or to become thin, to dissolve in fine parts, <hi type="italic">tabescere</hi>), like a worm-eaten decayed tree (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.20">Isa 40:20</reference>). The Talmud explains it thus, <hi type="italic">Joma</hi> 38b: foulness comes over their name, so that we call no one after their name. Also the idea suggests itself, that his name becomes corrupt, as it were, with his bones; the Mishnah, at least <hi type="italic">Ohaloth</hi> ii. 1, uses רקב of the dust of corruption.
entries.667ef363634b313fdae95dc38d5216628f7b964d: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.8">Pro 10:8</reference> <div eID="gen10897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10898" type="x-p"/> There follows now a series of proverbs in which reference to sins of the mouth and their contrary prevails: <div eID="gen10898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10899" type="x-p"/> He that is wise in heart receives precepts; <div eID="gen10899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10900" type="x-p"/> But he that is of a foolish mouth comes to ruin. <div eID="gen10900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10901" type="x-p"/> A חכם־לב, wise-hearted, as one whose heart is חכם, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.15">Pro 23:15</reference>; in a word, a נבון, a person of understanding or judgment, Pro 16:21. Such an one does not make his own knowledge the <hi type="italic">ne plus ultra</hi>, nor does he make his own will the <hi type="italic">noli me tangere</hi>; but he takes commands, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, instructions directing or prohibiting, to which he willingly subordinates himself as the outflow of a higher knowledge and will, and by which he sets bounds and limits to himself. But a fool of the lips, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, a braggart blunderer, one pleasing himself with vain talk (<reference osisRef="Prov.14.23">Pro 14:23</reference>), falls prostrate, for he thinks that he knows all things better, and will take no pattern; but while he boasts himself from on high, suddenly all at once - for he offends against the fundamental principle of common life and of morality - he comes to lie low down on the ground. The Syr. and Targ. translate ילּבט by, he is caught (Bertheau, ensnared); Aquila, Vulgate, Luther, δαρήσεται, he is slain; Symmachus, βασανισθήσεται; but all without any support in the usage of the language known to us. Theodotion, φυρήσεται, he is confounded, is not tenable; Joseph Kimchi, who after David Kimchi, under Hos 4:14, appeals in support of this meaning (ישׁתבשׁ, similarly Parchon: יתבלבל) to the Arabic, seems to think on iltibâs, confusion. The demonstrable meanings of the verb לבט are the following: 1. To occasion trouble. Thus <hi type="italic">Mechilta</hi>, under <reference osisRef="Exod.17.14">Exo 17:14</reference>, לבטוהו, one has imposed upon him trouble; Sifri, under Num 11:1, נתלבטנו, we are tired, according to which Rashi: he fatigues himself, but which fits neither to the subj. nor to the contrast, which is to be supposed. The same may be said of the meaning of the Syr. lbt, to drive on, to press, which without doubt accords with the former meaning of the word in the language of the Midrash. 2. In Arab. labaṭ (R. lab, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Wünsche’s Hos. p. 172), to throw any one down to the earth, so that he falls with his whole body his whole length; the passive נלבט, to be thus thrown down by another, or to throw oneself thus down, figuratively of one who falls hopelessly into evil and destruction (Fl.). The Arabic verb is also used of the springing run of the animal ridden on (to gallop), and of the being lame (to hop), according to which in the Lex. the explanations, he hurries, or he wavers hither and thither, are offered by Kimchi (<hi type="italic">Graec. Venet.</hi> πλανηθήσεται). But the former of these explanations, <hi type="italic">corruit</hi> (= <hi type="italic">in calamitatem ruit</hi>), placed much nearer by the Arabic, is confirmed by the lxx ὑποσκελισθήσεται, and by the <hi type="italic">Berêshith rabba</hi>, c. 52, where לבט is used in the sense to be ruined (= נכשׁל). Hitzig changes the passive into the active: “he throws the offered לקח scornfully to the ground,” but the contrast does not require this. The wanton, arrogant boasting lies already in the designation of the subj. אויל שׂפתים; and the sequel involves, as a consequence, the contrasted consequence of ready reception of the limitations and guidance of his own will by a higher.
entries.ddf9ed65ecebb8a74e9798f2decba612dda7453e: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.9">Pro 10:9</reference> <div eID="gen10901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10902" type="x-p"/> The form of this verse is like the eighth, word for word: <div eID="gen10902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10903" type="x-p"/> He that walketh in innocence walketh securely; <div eID="gen10903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10904" type="x-p"/> But he that goeth in secret ways is known. <div eID="gen10904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10905" type="x-p"/> The full form of בּתּום does not, as Hitzig supposes, stand in causal connection with the <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi>, for the consonant text lying before us is at least 500 years older than the accentuation. For הלך תּם at <reference osisRef="Prov.2.7">Pro 2:7</reference>, there is here הלך בּתּום = הלך בּדרך תום; so מעקּשׁ דּרכיו denotes, after <reference osisRef="Prov.2.15">Pro 2:15</reference>, such an one אשׁר דּרכיו עקּשׁים. Expressed in the language of the N.T., תום is the property of the ἁπλοῦς or ἀκέραιος, for the fundamental idea of fulness is here referred to full submission, full integrity. Such an one goes בּטח (Aquila, ἀμερίμνως), for there is nothing designedly concealed by him, of which he has reason to fear that it will come to the light; whoever, on the contrary, makes his ways crooked, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, turns into crooked ways, is perceived, or, as we might also explain it (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Gen.4.15">Gen 4:15</reference>): if one (<hi type="italic">qui</hi> = <hi type="italic">si quis</hi>) makes his ways crooked, then it is known - nothing, however, stands opposed to the reference of יוּדע to the person: he is finally known, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, unmasked (lxx Jerome, γνωσθήσεται, <hi type="italic">manifestus fiet</hi>). Usually it is explained: he is knowing, clever, with the remark that נודע is here the passive of הודיע (Gesen., Ewald, Hitzig); <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. to give to feel; <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. to become to feel, properly to be made to know (Luth.: made wise); but the passive of the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. is the <hi type="italic">Hoph</hi>. Such a <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. in which the causative (not simply transitive) signification of the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. would be applied passively is without example (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Ewald, §133a); the meaning of <reference osisRef="Jer.31.19">Jer 31:19</reference> also is: after I have become known, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, been made manifest, uncovered, drawn into the light.
entries.6c082849829de465f9f6632c30ca236e3f5d6d52: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.10">Pro 10:10</reference> <div eID="gen10905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10906" type="x-p"/> This verse contains another proverb, similarly formed, parallel with the half of <reference osisRef="Prov.10.8">Pro 10:8</reference> : <div eID="gen10906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10907" type="x-p"/> He that winketh with the eye causeth trouble; <div eID="gen10907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10908" type="x-p"/> And a foolish mouth comes to ruin. <div eID="gen10908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10909" type="x-p"/> Regarding the winking or nipping, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the repeated nipping of the eyes (cf. <hi type="italic">nictare</hi>, frequent. of <hi type="italic">nicere</hi>), as the conduct of the malicious or malignant, which aims at the derision or injury of him to whom it refers, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Prov.6.13">Pro 6:13</reference>; there קרץ was connected with ב of the means of the action; here, as <reference osisRef="Ps.35.19">Psa 35:19</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.16.30">Pro 16:30</reference>, it is connected with the object accus. He who so does produces trouble (heart-sorrow, <reference osisRef="Prov.15.13">Pro 15:13</reference>), whether it be that he who is the butt of this mockery marks it, or that he is the victim of secretly concerted injury; יתּן is not here used impersonally, as <reference osisRef="Prov.13.10">Pro 13:10</reference>, but as <reference osisRef="Prov.29.15">Pro 29:15</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.19.28">Lev 19:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.24.20">Lev 24:20</reference>, in the sense of the cause. 10b forms a striking contrast to 10a, according to the text of the lxx: ὁ δὲ ἐλεγχων μετὰ παῤῥησίας εἰρηνοποιεῖ, contrary to the Syr., by the Hebrew text, which certainly is older than this its correction, which Ewald and Lagarde unsuccessfully attempt to translate into the Hebrew. The foolish mouth, here understood in conformity with 10a, is one who talks at random, without examination and deliberation, and thus suddenly stumbles and falls over, so that he comes to lie on the ground, to his own disgrace and injury.
entries.ae468d8400a5e35660e36fde0059a76d07d93834: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.11">Pro 10:11</reference> <div eID="gen10909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10910" type="x-p"/> Another proverb, similar to the half of <reference osisRef="Prov.10.6">Pro 10:6</reference> : <div eID="gen10910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10911" type="x-p"/> A fountain of life is the mouth of the righteous; <div eID="gen10911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10912" type="x-p"/> But the mouth of the godless hideth violence. <div eID="gen10912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10913" type="x-p"/> If we understand 11b wholly as 6b: <hi type="italic">os improborum obteget violentia</hi>, then the meaning of 11a would be, that that which the righteous speaks tends to his own welfare (Fl.). But since the words spoken are the means of communication and of intercourse, one has to think of the water as welling up in one, and flowing forth to another; and the meaning of 11b has to accommodate itself to the preceding half proverb, whereby it cannot be mistaken that חמס (violence), which was 6b subj., bears here, by the contrast, the stamp of the obj.; for the possibility of manifold windings and turnings is a characteristic of the Mashal. In the Psalms and Prophets it is God who is called מקור חיּים, <reference osisRef="Ps.36.10">Psa 36:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.13">Jer 2:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.17.13">Jer 17:13</reference>; the proverbial poetry plants the figure on ethical ground, and understands by it a living power, from which wholesome effects accrue to its possessor, <reference osisRef="Prov.14.27">Pro 14:27</reference>, and go forth from him to others, Pro 13:14. Thus the mouth of the righteous is here called a fountain of life, because that which he speaks, and as he speaks it, is morally strengthening, intellectually elevating, and inwardly quickening in its effect on the hearers; while, on the contrary, the mouth of the godless covereth wrong (<hi type="italic">violentiam</hi>), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, conceals with deceitful words the intention, directed not to that which is best, but to the disadvantage and ruin of his neighbours; so that words which in the one case bring to light a ground of life and of love, and make it effectual, in the other case serve for a covering to an immoral, malevolent background.
entries.8e213984670d4971964468c9fd18370fe8503ac1: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.12">Pro 10:12</reference> <div eID="gen10913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10914" type="x-p"/> Another proverb of the different effects of hatred and of love: <div eID="gen10914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10915" type="x-p"/> Hate stirreth up strife, <div eID="gen10915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10916" type="x-p"/> And love covereth all transgressions. <div eID="gen10916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10917" type="x-p"/> Regarding מדנים, for which the Kerı̂ elsewhere substitutes מדינים, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under Pro 6:14. Hatred of one’s neighbour, which is of itself an evil, has further this bad effect, that it calls forth hatred, and thus stirreth up strife, feuds, factions, for it incites man against man (cf. ערר, <reference osisRef="Job.3.8">Job 3:8</reference>); on the contrary, love covers not merely little errors, but also greater sins of every kind (כּל־פּשׁעים), viz., by pardoning them, concealing them, excusing them, if possible, with mitigating circumstances, or restraining them before they are executed. All this lies in the covering. James, however, gives it, Jam 5:20, another rendering: love covers them, viz., from the eyes of a holy God; for it forgives them to the erring brother, and turns him from the error of his way. The lxx improperly translate πάντας δὲ τοὺς μὴ φιλονεικοῦντας κελόπτει φιλία; but Peter (1Pe 4:8) as well as James, but none of the Greek versions; ἡ ἀγάπη καλύψει πλῆθος ἁμαρτιῶν. The Romish Church makes use of this passage as a proof for the introduction of the <hi type="italic">fides formata</hi>, viz., <hi type="italic">caritate</hi>, in justification, which is condemned in the Apology of the Augsburg Confession; and, indeed, the <hi type="italic">multitudo peccatorum</hi> is not meant of the sins of him who cherishes love, but of the sins of the neighbour. Sin stirs up hatred in men in their relation to one another; but love covers the already existing sins, and smooths the disturbances occasioned by them.
entries.64daf0b3e804b33f01f5d49ea3d3dac9ccffbcd5: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.13">Pro 10:13</reference> <div eID="gen10917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10918" type="x-p"/> There follow now two other proverbs on the use and abuse of speech: <div eID="gen10918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10919" type="x-p"/> On the lips of the man of understanding wisdom is found; <div eID="gen10919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10920" type="x-p"/> And the rod for the back of the fool. <div eID="gen10920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10921" type="x-p"/> With Löwenstein, Hitzig, and others, it is inadmissible to regard ושׁבט as a second subject to תּמּצא. The mouth itself, or the word of the mouth, may be called a rod, viz., a rod of correction (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.4">Isa 11:4</reference>); but that wisdom and such a rod are found on the lips of the wise would be a combination and a figure in bad taste. Thus 13b is a clause by itself, as Luther renders it: “but a rod belongs to the fool’s back;” and this will express a contrast to 13a, that while wisdom is to be sought for on the lips of the man of understanding (cf. Mal 2:7), a man devoid of understanding, on the contrary, gives himself to such hollow and corrupt talk, that in order to educate him to something better, if possible, the rod must be applied to his back; for, according to the Talmudic proverb: that which a wise man gains by a hint, a fool only obtains by a club. The rod is called שׁבט, from שׁבט, to be smooth, to go straight down (as the hair of the head); and the back גּו, from גּוה, to be rounded, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, concave or convex.
entries.502e288928bdc68a780dfa9ce2c993a87eab39c7: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.14">Pro 10:14</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.10.14">14</reference> Wise men store up knowledge;      But the mouth of the fool is threatening destruction. <div eID="gen10921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10922" type="x-p"/> Ewald, Bertheau, Hitzig, Oetinger: “The mouth of the fool blunders out, and is as the sudden falling in of a house which one cannot escape from.” But since מחתּה is a favourite <hi type="italic">Mishle</hi>-word to denote the effect and issue of that which is dangerous and destructive, so the sense is perhaps further to be extended: the mouth of the fool is for himself (<reference osisRef="Prov.13.3">Pro 13:3</reference>) and others a near, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, an always threatening and unexpectedly occurring calamity; unexpectedly, because suddenly he blunders out with his inconsiderate shame-bringing talk, so that such a fool’s mouth is to every one a <hi type="italic">praesens periculum</hi>. As to יצפּנוּ, it is worthy of remark that in the Beduin, Arab. dfn, <hi type="italic">fut. i</hi>, signifies to be still, to be thoughtful, to be absorbed in oneself (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Wetstein on Job, p. 281). According to Codd. and editions, in this correct, וּפי־ is to be written instead of אויל uwpiy; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Baer’s <hi type="italic">Torath Emeth</hi>, p. 40.
entries.116c08dab05dc754e03bc8ede5aecc2ab30833af: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.15">Pro 10:15</reference> <div eID="gen10922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10923" type="x-p"/> A pair of proverbs regarding possession and gain. <div eID="gen10923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10924" type="x-p"/> Regarding possession: <div eID="gen10924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10925" type="x-p"/> The rich man’s wealth is his strong city; <div eID="gen10925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10926" type="x-p"/> The destruction of the poor is their poverty. <div eID="gen10926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10927" type="x-p"/> The first line = Pro 18:11. One may render the idea according to that which is internal, and according to that which is external; and the proverb remains in both cases true. As עז may mean, of itself alone, power, as means of protection, or a bulwark (<reference osisRef="Ps.8.3">Psa 8:3</reference>), or the consciousness of power, high feeling, pride (Jdg 5:21); so קרית עזּו may be rendered as an object of self-confidence, and מחתּה, on the contrary, as an object of terror (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.39">Jer 48:39</reference>): the rich man, to whom his estate (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., on הון, p. 63) affords a sure reserve and an abundant source of help, can appear confident and go forth energetically; on the contrary, the poor man is timid and bashful, and is easily dejected and discouraged. Thus <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Oetinger and Hitzig. But the objective interpretation is allowable, and lies also much nearer: the rich man stands thus independent, changes and adversities cannot so easily overthrow him, he is also raised above many hazards and temptations; on the contrary, the poor man is overthrown by little misfortunes, and his despairing endeavours to save himself, when they fail, ruin him completely, and perhaps make him at the same time a moral outlaw. It is quite an experienced fact which this proverb expresses, but one from which the double doctrine is easily derived: (1) That it is not only advised, but also commanded, that man make the firm establishing of his external life-position the aim of his endeavour; (2) That one ought to treat with forbearance the humble man; and if he always sinks deeper and deeper, one ought not to judge him with unmerciful harshness and in proud self-exaltation.
entries.980ef8e3e2e09eff5acbaf953b8fa800f6249ade: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.16">Pro 10:16</reference> <div eID="gen10927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10928" type="x-p"/> Regarding gain: <div eID="gen10928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10929" type="x-p"/> The gain of the righteous tendeth to life; <div eID="gen10929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10930" type="x-p"/> The income of the godless to sin. <div eID="gen10930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10931" type="x-p"/> Intentionally, that which the righteous received is called פּעלּה (as <reference osisRef="Lev.19.13">Lev 19:13</reference>), as a reward of his labour; that which the godless receives is called תּבוּאה, as income which does not need to be the reward of labour, and especially of his own immediate labour. And with לחיּים, לחטּאת runs parallel, from the supposition that sin carries the germ of death in itself. The reward of his labour serves to the righteous to establish his life, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, to make sure his life-position, and to elevate his life-happiness. On the contrary, the income of the godless serves only to ruin his life; for, made thereby full and confident, he adds sin to sin, whose wages is death. Hitzig translates: for expiation, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, to lose it again as atonement for past sins; but if חיים and חטאת are contrasted with each other, then חטאת is death-bringing sin (Pro 8:35.).
entries.185765e1099dd4f30b246ee7b280d420dcd35cb5: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.17">Pro 10:17</reference> <div eID="gen10931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10932" type="x-p"/> The group of proverbs now following bring again to view the good and bad effects of human speech. The seventeenth verse introduces the transition: 17 There is a way to life when one gives heed to correction;      And whoever disregards instruction runs into error. <div eID="gen10932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10933" type="x-p"/> Instead of ארח חיּים (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.6">Pro 5:6</reference>), there is here ארח לחיים; and then this proverb falls into rank with <reference osisRef="Prov.10.16">Pro 10:16</reference>, which contains the same word לחיים. The accentuation denotes ארח as subst.; for ארח way, road = ארח [a wayfarer, part. of ארח] would, as שׁסע, <reference osisRef="Lev.11.7">Lev 11:7</reference>, נטע, <reference osisRef="Ps.94.9">Psa 94:9</reference>, have the tone on the ultima. It is necessary neither to change the tone, nor, with Ewald, to interpret ארח as <hi type="italic">abstr. pro concreto</hi>, like הלך, for the expression “wanderer to life” has no support in the <hi type="italic">Mishle</hi>. Michaelis has given the right interpretation: <hi type="italic">via ad vitam est si quis custodiat disciplinam</hi>. The syntactical contents, however, are different, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.13">1Sa 2:13</reference>, where the participle has the force of a hypothetical clause; for the expression: “a way to life is he who observes correction,” is equivalent to: he is on the way to life who...; a variety of the manner of expression: “the porch was twenty cubits,” <reference osisRef="2Chr.3.4">2Ch 3:4</reference>, particularly adapted to the figurative language of proverbial poetry, as if the poet said: See there one observant of correction - that (viz., the שׁמר [שׁמר, to watch] representing itself in this שׁמר) is the way to life. מוּסר and תּוכחת are related to each other as παιδεία and ἔλεγχος; עזב [עזב, to leave, forsake] is equivalent to בּלתּי שׁמר. מתעה would be unsuitable as a contrast in the causative sense: who guides wrong, according to which Bertheau understands 17a, that only he who observes correction can guide others to life. We expect to hear what injuries he who thinks to raise himself above all reproach brings on himself. Hitzig, in his Commentary (1858), for this reason places the <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. מתּעה (rather write מתּעה) in the place of the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>.; but in the <hi type="italic">Comm. on Jeremiah</hi> (1866), 42:20, he rightly remarks: “To err, not as an involuntary condition, but as an arbitrary proceeding, is suitably expressed by the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>.” In like manner הוסיף, הגּיע (to touch), הרחיק (to go to a distance), denote the active conduct of a being endowed with reason; Ewald, §122, c. Jewish interpreters gloss מתעה by supplying נפשׁו; but it signifies only as inwardly transitive, to accomplish the action of the תּעות.
entries.9ad9cb95fd1bf0b894c3b62da2bcbbd420812465: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.18">Pro 10:18</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.10.18">18</reference> He that hideth hatred is a mouth of falsehood;      And he that spreadeth slander is a fool. <div eID="gen10933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10934" type="x-p"/> The lxx, καλύπτουσιν ἔχθραν χεῖλα δίκαια, which Ewald prefers, and which has given occasion to Hitzig to make a remarkable conjecture (“He who conceals hatred, close lips,” which no one understands without Hitzig’s comment. to this his conjecture). But (1) to hide hatred (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.10.11">Pro 10:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.26.24">Pro 26:24</reference>) is something altogether different from to cover sin (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.12">Pro 10:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.17.9">Pro 17:9</reference>), or generally to keep anything secret with discretion (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.13">Pro 10:13</reference>); and (2) that δίκαια is a corrupt reading for ἄδικα (as Grabe supposes, and Symmachus translates) or δόλια (as Lagarde supposes, and indeed is found in Codd.). Michaelis well remarks: <hi type="italic">odium tectum est dolosi, manifesta sycophantia stultorum</hi>. Whoever conceals hateful feelings behind his words is שׂפתי־שׂקר, a mouth of falsehood (cf. the mouth of the fool, <reference osisRef="Prov.10.14">Pro 10:14</reference>); one does not need to supply אישׁ, but much rather has hence to conclude that a false man is simply so named, as is proved by Psa 120:3. There is a second moral judgment, 18b: he who spreadeth slander (וּמוצא, according to the Masoretic writing: he who divulges it, the correlate to הביא, to bring to, <reference osisRef="Gen.37.2">Gen 37:2</reference>) is a <hi type="italic">Thor</hi> fool, stupid, dull, כּסיל (not a <hi type="italic">Narr</hi> fool, godless person, אויל); for such slandering can generally bring no advantage; it injures the reputation of him to whom the דבּה, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the secret report, the slander, refers; it sows discord, has incalculable consequences, and finally brings guilt on the tale-bearer himself.
entries.b6b71075195a09c6bdb54914d40c45db55eff4bb: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.19">Pro 10:19</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.10.19">19</reference> In a multitude of words transgression is not wanting;      But he who restrains his lips shows wisdom. <div eID="gen10934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10935" type="x-p"/> We do not, with Bertheau, understand 19a: by many words a transgression does not cease to be what it is; the contrast 19b requires a more general condemnation of the multitude of words, and חדל not only means to cease from doing (to leave off), and to cease from being (to take away), but also not at all to do (to intermit, <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.11">Eze 3:11</reference>; Zec 11:12), and not at all to be (to fail, to be absent), thus: <hi type="italic">ubi verborum est abundantia non deest peccatum</hi> (Fl.). Michaelis suitably compares πολυλογία πολλὰ σφάλματα ἒχει by Stobäus, and כל המרבה דברים מביא חטא in the tractate <hi type="italic">Aboth</hi> i. 17, wherewith Rashi explains the proverb. פּשׁע is not here, as elsewhere, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.19.14">Psa 19:14</reference>, with special reference to the sin of falling away from favour, apostasy, but, like the post-biblical עברה, generally with reference to every kind of violation (פשׁע = Arab. fsq <hi type="italic">dirumpere</hi>) of moral restraint; here, as Jansen remarks, <hi type="italic">peccatum sive mendacii, sive detractionis, sive alterius indiscretae laesionis, sive vanitatis, sive denique verbi otiosi</hi>. In 19b it is more appropriate to regard משׂכּיל as the present of the internal transitive (<hi type="italic">intelligenter agit</hi>) than to interpret it in the attributive sense (<hi type="italic">intelligens</hi>).
entries.950fe2065adcba82a0b37dcc366b3a6b438da7a2: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.20">Pro 10:20</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.10.20">20</reference> Choice silver is the tongue of the righteous;      But the heart of the godless is little worth. <div eID="gen10935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10936" type="x-p"/> Choice silver is, as <reference osisRef="Prov.8.19">Pro 8:19</reference>, cf. 10, pure, freed from all base mixtures. Like it, pure and noble, is whatever the righteous speaks; the heart, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the manner of thought and feeling, of the godless is, on the contrary, like little <hi type="italic">instar nihili</hi>, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, of little or no worth, Arab. yasway kâlyla (Fl.). lxx: the heart of the godless ἐκλείψει, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, ימעט, at first arrogant and full of lofty plans, it becomes always the more dejected, discouraged, empty. But 20a leads us to expect some designation of its worth. The Targ. (according to which the Peshito is to be corrected; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Levy’s Wörterbuch, ii. 26): the heart of the godless is מחתא (from נחת), refuse, dross. The other Greek versions accord with the text before us.
entries.ff1c27391b4458a72e035eed5aa2c81a9e73e183: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.21">Pro 10:21</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.10.21">21</reference> The lips of the righteous edify many;      But fools die through want of understanding. <div eID="gen10936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10937" type="x-p"/> The lxx translate 21a: the lips of the righteous ἐπίσταται ὑψηλά, which would at least require ידעו רבות. רעה is, like the post-bibl. pir|neec (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., the Hebr. <hi type="italic">Römerbrief</hi>, p. 97), another figure for the N.T. οἰκοδομεῖν: to afford spiritual nourishment and strengthening, to which Fleischer compares the ecclesiastical expressions: <hi type="italic">pastor</hi>, <hi type="italic">ovile ecclesiae, les ouailles</hi>; רעה means leader, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.21">Jer 10:21</reference>, as well as teacher, <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.11">Ecc 12:11</reference>, for it contains partly the prevailing idea of leading, partly of feeding. ירעוּ stands for תּרעינה, as <reference osisRef="Prov.10.32">Pro 10:32</reference>, Pro 5:2. In 21b, Bertheau incorrectly explains, as Euchel and Michaelis: <hi type="italic">stulti complures per dementem unum moriuntur</hi>; the food has truly enough in his own folly, and needs not to be first drawn by others into destruction. חסר is not here the connective form of חסר (Jewish interpreters: for that reason, that he is such an one), nor of חסר (Hitzig, Zöckler), which denotes, as a concluded idea, <hi type="italic">penuria</hi>, but like רחב, <reference osisRef="Prov.21.4">Pro 21:4</reference>, שׁכב, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.10">Pro 6:10</reference>, and שׁפל, <reference osisRef="Prov.16.19">Pro 16:19</reference>, infin.: they die by want of understanding (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.5.23">Pro 5:23</reference>); this <hi type="italic">amentia</hi> is the cause of their death, for it leads fools to meet destruction without their observing it (Hos 4:6).
entries.ea751535c7811ed1bb5fdafea24ed527f3129bb0: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.22">Pro 10:22</reference> <div eID="gen10937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10938" type="x-p"/> Three proverbs which say that good comes from above, and is as a second nature to the man of understanding: 22 Jahve’s blessing - it maketh rich;      And labour addeth nothing thereto <div eID="gen10938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10939" type="x-p"/> Like 24a, היא limits the predicate to this and no other subject: “all depends on God’s blessing.” Here is the first half of the <hi type="italic">ora et labora</hi>. The proverb is a compendium of <reference osisRef="Ps.127.1">Psa 127:1</reference>-2. 22b is to be understood, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.127.2">Psa 127:2</reference> of this Solomonic psalm, not that God adds to His blessing no sorrow, much rather with the possession grants at the same time a joyful, peaceful mind (lxx, Targ., Syriac, Jerome, Aben-Ezra, Michaelis, and others), which would require the word עליה; but that trouble, labour, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, strenuous self-endeavours, add not (anything) to it, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, that it does not associate itself with the blessing (which, as the Jewish interpreters rightly remark, is, according to its nature, תוספת, as the curse is חסרון) as the <hi type="italic">causa efficiens</hi>, or if we supply <hi type="italic">quidquam</hi>, as the complement to עמּהּ along with it: nothing is added thereto, which goes along with that which the blessing of God grants, and completes it. Thus correctly Rashi, Luther, Ziegler, Ewald, Hitzig, Zöckler. the now current accentuation, לאו יוסף עצב עמּהּ, is incorrect. Older editions, as Venice 1525, 1615, Basel 1618, have ולא־יוסף עצב עמה, the transformation of ולא־יוסף עצב. Besides, עצב has double <hi type="italic">Segol</hi> (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Kimchi’s Lex.), and יוסף is written, according to the Masora, in the first syllable <hi type="italic">plene</hi>, in the last <hi type="italic">defective</hi>.
entries.8273882029108271ba15d5c69da537480b68548c: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.23">Pro 10:23</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.10.23">23</reference> Like sport to a fool is the commission of a crime;      And wisdom to a man of understanding. <div eID="gen10939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10940" type="x-p"/> Otherwise Löwenstein: to a fool the carrying out of a plan is as sport; to the man of understanding, on the contrary, as wisdom. זמּה, from זמם, to press together, mentally to think, as <reference osisRef="Job.17.11">Job 17:11</reference>, and according to Gesenius, also <reference osisRef="Prov.21.27">Pro 21:27</reference>; Pro 24:9. But זמּה has the prevailing signification of an outrage against morality, a sin of unchastity; and especially the phrase עשׂה זמּה is in Jdg 20:6 and in Ezekiel not otherwise used, so that all the old interpreters render it here by <hi type="italic">patrare scelus</hi>; only the Targum has the equivocal עבד עבידתּא; the Syriac, however, 'bd bı̂ taa'. Sinful conduct appears to the fool, who places himself above the solemnity of the moral law, as sport; and wisdom, on the contrary, (appears as sport) to a man of understanding. We would not venture on this acceptation of כּשׂחוק if שׂחק were not attributed, Pro 8:30., to wisdom itself. This alternate relationship recommends itself by the indetermination of חכמהו, which is not favourable to the interpretation: <hi type="italic">sed sapientiam colit vir intelligens</hi>, or as Jerome has it: <hi type="italic">sapientia autem est viro prudentia</hi>. The subjects of the antithesis chiastically combine within the verse: חכמה, in contrast to wicked conduct, is acting in accordance with moral principles. This to the man of understanding is as easy as sporting, just as to the fool is shameless sinning; for he follows in this an inner impulse, it brings to him joy, it is the element in which he feels himself satisfied.
entries.6021f2368de69afaa4c8a79ff1efbd271f7f16f3: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.24">Pro 10:24</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.10.24">24</reference> That of which the godless is afraid cometh upon him,      And what the righteous desires is granted to him. <div eID="gen10940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10941" type="x-p"/> The formation of the clause 24a is like the similar proverb, <reference osisRef="Prov.11.27">Pro 11:27</reference>; the subject-idea has there its expression in the genitival <hi type="italic">annexum</hi>, of which <reference osisRef="Gen.9.6">Gen 9:6</reference> furnishes the first example; in this passage before us it stands at the beginning, and is, as in <reference osisRef="Prov.10.22">Pro 10:22</reference>, emphatically repeated with היא. מגורה, properly the turning oneself away, hence shrinking back in terror; here, as <reference osisRef="Isa.66.4">Isa 66:4</reference>, of the object of fear, parallel to תּאוה, wishing, of the object of the wish. In 24b Ewald renders יתּן as adj. from יתן (whence איתן ecne), after the form פּקּח, and translates: yet to the righteous desire is always green. But whether יתּן is probably formed from יתן, and not from נתן, is a question in <reference osisRef="Prov.12.12">Pro 12:12</reference>, but not here, where wishing and giving (fulfilling) are naturally <hi type="italic">correlata</hi>. Hitzig corrects יתּן, and certainly the supplying of 'ה is as little appropriate here as at Pro 13:21. Also a “one gives” is scarcely intended (according to which the Targ., Syr., and Jerome translate passively), in which case the Jewish interpreters are wont to explain יתן, scil. הנותן; for if the poet thought of יתן fo with a personal subject, why did he not rescue it from the dimness of such vague generality? Thus, then, יתן is, with Böttcher, to be interpreted as impersonal, like <reference osisRef="Prov.13.10">Pro 13:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.37.10">Job 37:10</reference>, and perhaps also <reference osisRef="Gen.38.28">Gen 38:28</reference> (Ewald, §295a): what the righteous wish, that there is, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, it becomes actual, is fulfilled. In this we have not directly and exclusively to think of the destiny at which the godless are afraid (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.27">Heb 10:27</reference>), and toward which the desire of the righteous goes forth; but the clause has also truth which is realized in this world: just that which they greatly fear, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, sickness, bankruptcy, the loss of reputation, comes upon the godless; on the contrary that which the righteous wish realizes itself, because their wish, in its intention, and kind, and content, stands in harmony with the order of the moral world.
entries.d341074d8baab946dc98985f4cfc6d728c5be4f5: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.25">Pro 10:25</reference> <div eID="gen10941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10942" type="x-p"/> There now follows a series of proverbs, broken by only one dissimilar proverb, on the immoveable continuance of the righteous: 25 When the storm sweeps past, it is no more with the wicked;      But the righteous is a building firm for ever. <div eID="gen10942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10943" type="x-p"/> How <reference osisRef="Prov.10.25">Pro 10:25</reference> is connected with <reference osisRef="Prov.10.24">Pro 10:24</reference> is shown in the Book of Wisdom 5:15 (the hope of the wicked like chaff which the wind pursues). The Aram., Jerome, and <hi type="italic">Graec. Venet.</hi> interpret כ of comparison, so that the destruction of the godless is compared in suddenness and rapidity to the rushing past of a storm; but then רוּח ought to have been used instead of סוּפה; and instead of ואין רשׁע with the ו <hi type="italic">apodosis</hi>, a disturbing element in such a comparison, would have been used יחלף רשׁע, or at least רשׁע אין. The thought is no other than that of <reference osisRef="Job.21.18">Job 21:18</reference> : the storm, which is called סופה, from סוּף, to rush forth, is meant, as sweeping forth, and כ the temporal, as <reference osisRef="Exod.11.4">Exo 11:4</reference> (lxx παραπορευομένης καταιγίδος), with ו htiw ,)עןה <hi type="italic">apod</hi>. following, like <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, after a similar member of a temporal sentence, Isa 10:25. סופה is a figure of God-decreed calamities, as war and pestilence, under which the godless sink, while the righteous endure them; cf. with 25a, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.27">Pro 1:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.18">Isa 28:18</reference>; and with 25b, <reference osisRef="Isa.3.25">Isa 3:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.4">Hab 2:4</reference>; Psa 91:1. “An everlasting foundation,” since עולם is understood as looking forwards, not as at <reference osisRef="Isa.58.12">Isa 58:12</reference>, backwards, is a foundation capable of being shaken by nothing, and synecdoch. generally a building. The proverb reminds us of the close of the Sermon on the Mount, and finds the final confirmation of its truth in this, that the death of the godless is a penal thrusting of them away, but the death of the righteous a lifting them up to their home. The righteous also often enough perish in times of war and of pestilence; but the proverb, as it is interpreted, verifies itself, even although not so as the poet, viewing it from his narrow O.T. standpoint, understood it; for the righteous, let him die when and how he may, is preserved, while the godless perishes.
entries.19dec4bd2041a293354472f95fb1103af2a0a503: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.26">Pro 10:26</reference> <div eID="gen10943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10944" type="x-p"/> This proverb stands out of connection with the series: <div eID="gen10944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10945" type="x-p"/> As vinegar to the teeth, and as smoke to the eyes, <div eID="gen10945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10946" type="x-p"/> So is the sluggard to them who gives him a commission. <div eID="gen10946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10947" type="x-p"/> A parabolic proverb (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., p. 9), <hi type="italic">priamel</hi>-like in its formation (p. 13). Here and there לשּׁנּים is found with <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi>, but in correct texts it has <hi type="italic">Rebîa-magnum</hi>; the verse is divided into two by <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi>, whose subordinate distributive is (<hi type="italic">Accentssystem</hi>, xi. §1) <hi type="italic">Rebîa-magnum</hi>. Smoke makes itself disagreeably perceptible to the sense of smell, and particularly to the eyes, which it causes to smart so that they overflow with tears; wherefore Virgil speaks of it as <hi type="italic">amarus</hi>, and Horace <hi type="italic">lacrimosus</hi>. חמץ (from חמץ, to be sour, harsh) signifies properly that which is sour, as <hi type="italic">acetum</hi>, ὄξος; here, after the lxx ὄμφαξ, the unripe grapes, but which are called בּסר (בּסר) (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Job.15.33">Job 15:33</reference>), by which the Syr., here following the lxx, translates, and which also in the Talmud, Demaï i. 1, is named חמץ, after a doubtful meaning (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Aruch, and on the other side Rashi), thus: vinegar, which the word commonly means, and which also accords with the object of the comparison, especially if one thinks of the sharp vinegar-wine of the south, which has an effect on the teeth denoted by the Hebr. verb קהה, as the effect of smoke is by כהה (Fl.). The plur. לשׁלחיו is that of the category, like <reference osisRef="Prov.22.21">Pro 22:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.25.13">Pro 25:13</reference>; the parallel אדניו of the latter passage does not at least make it necessary to regard it, like this, as a <hi type="italic">plur. excellentiae</hi> (Bertheau, Hitzig, Ewald). They who send a sluggard, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, who make him their agent, do it to their own sorrow; his slothfulness is for them, and for that which they have in view, of dull, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, slow and restrained, of biting, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, sensibly injurious operation.
entries.d8357ebecbbbab8af10316586956bd20a77ac3d9: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.27">Pro 10:27</reference> <div eID="gen10947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10948" type="x-p"/> From this point the proverbs fall into the series connecting themselves with <reference osisRef="Prov.10.25">Pro 10:25</reference> : <reference osisRef="Prov.10.27">27</reference> The fear of Jahve multiplies the days of life;      But the years of the godless are shortened. <div eID="gen10948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10949" type="x-p"/> This parable, like <reference osisRef="Prov.10.25">Pro 10:25</reference>, also corresponds with the O.T. standpoint, having in view the present life. The present-life history confirms it, for vice destroys body and soul; and the fear of God, which makes men contented and satisfied in God, is truly the right principle of longevity. But otherwise also the pious often enough die early, for God carries them away מפני הרעה from the face of the evil, Isa 57:1.; or if they are martyrs for the truth (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.23">Psa 44:23</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.60.6">Psa 60:6</reference>), the verification of the above proverb in such cases moves forward (Wisd. 4:7ff.) into eternity, in which the life of the pious continues for ever, while that of the godless loses itself with his death in the state of everlasting death. <reference osisRef="Prov.9.11">Pro 9:11</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.3.2">Pro 3:2</reference>, resembles 27a. Instead of תּקצרנה, תקצרנה was to be expected; but the flexion does not distinguish the transitive קצר (Arab. ḳaṣara) and intransitive קצר (Arab. ḳaṣura) as it ought.
entries.303d35e8baa1e49e1eab6b4f351285f18b1d3063: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.28">Pro 10:28</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.10.28">28</reference> The expectation of the righteous is gladness      And the hope of the godless comes to nothing. תּוחלת as well as תּקוה proceed on the fundamental idea of a strained earnest looking back upon something, the same fundamental idea which in another view gives the meaning of strength (חיל, Arab. ḥayl; ḳuwwat, kawiyy, cf. גּדל, Arab. jdl, <hi type="italic">plectere</hi>, and גּדול, strong and strength). The substantival clause 28a denotes nothing more than: it is gladness (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.3.17">Pro 3:17</reference>, all their steps are gladness), but which is equivalent to, it is that in its issue, <hi type="italic">in gaudium desinit</hi>. Hitzig’s remark that תוחלת is the chief idea for hope and fear, is not confirmed by the usage of the language; it always signifies joyful, not anxious, expectation; cf. the interchange of the same two synonyms <reference osisRef="Prov.13.7">Pro 13:7</reference>, and תּאות, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.10">Psa 112:10</reference>, instead of תּקות (here and <reference osisRef="Job.8.13">Job 8:13</reference>). While the expectation of the one terminates in the joy of the fulfilment, the hope of the other (אבד, R. בד, to separate) perishes, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, comes to nothing.
entries.e1d0fd013c98b402629c252982f5752e302c1e1d: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.29">Pro 10:29</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.10.29">29</reference> Jahve’s way is a bulwark to the righteous;      But ruin to those that do evil. <div eID="gen10949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10950" type="x-p"/> Of the two meanings which מעז (מעוז) has: a stronghold from עזז, and asylum (= Arab. m'adz) from עוּז, the contrast here demands the former. 'דּרך ה and 'יראת ה, understood objectively, are the two O.T. names of true religion. It means, then, the way which the God of revelation directs men to walk in (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.8">Psa 143:8</reference>), the way of His precepts, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.27">Psa 119:27</reference>, His way of salvation, <reference osisRef="Ps.67.3">Psa 67:3</reference> (<reference osisRef="Ps.67.4">4</reference>); in the N.T. ἡ ὁδὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.16">Mat 22:16</reference>; Act 18:25.; cf. ἡ ὁδός simply, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.2">Act 9:2</reference>; Act 24:14. This way of Jahve is a fortress, bulwark, defence for innocence, or more precisely, a disposition wholly, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, unreservedly and without concealment, directed toward God and that which is good. All the old interpreters, also Luther, but not the <hi type="italic">Graec. Venet.</hi>, translate as if the expression were לתּם; but the punctuation has preferred the <hi type="italic">abstr. pro concreto</hi>, perhaps because the personal תּם nowhere else occurs with any such prefix; on the contrary, תּם is frequently connected with ב, כ, ל. לתם דרך, <hi type="italic">integro viae</hi> (<hi type="italic">vitae</hi>), are by no means to be connected in one conception (Ziegler, Umbr., Elster), for then the poet ought to have written מעז יהוה לתם־דרך. 29b cannot be interpreted as a thought by itself: and ruin (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding מחתּה, <hi type="italic">ruina</hi>, and subjectively <hi type="italic">consternatio</hi>, <reference osisRef="Prov.10.16">Pro 10:16</reference>) comes to those who do evil; but the thought, much more comprehensive, that religion, which is for the righteous a strong protection and safe retreat, will be an overthrow to those who delight only in wickedness (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., on און, p. 143), is confirmed by the similarly formed distich, Pro 21:15. Also almost all the Jewish interpreters, from Rashi to Malbim, find here expressed the operation of the divine revelation set over against the conduct of men - essentially the same as when the Tora or the Chokma present to men for their choice life and death; or the gospel of salvation, according to <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.15">2Co 2:15</reference>, is to one the savour of life unto life, to another the savour of death unto death.
entries.554869caea0c1849204ad142180a222266395a69: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.30">Pro 10:30</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.10.30">30</reference> The righteous is never moved;      But the godless abide not in the land. <div eID="gen10950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10951" type="x-p"/> Love of home is an impulse and emotion natural to man; but to no people was fatherland so greatly delighted in, to none was exile and banishment from fatherland so dreadful a thought, as it was to the people of Israel. Expatriation is the worst of all evils with which the prophets threatened individuals and the people, <reference osisRef="Amos.7.17">Amo 7:17</reference>, cf. Isa 22:17.; and the history of Israel in their exile, which was a punishment of their national apostasy, confirms this proverb and explains its form; cf. Pro 2:21., Psa 37:29. בּל is, like <reference osisRef="Prov.9.13">Pro 9:13</reference>, the emphatic No of the more elevated style; נמוט, the opposite of נכון, <reference osisRef="Prov.12.3">Pro 12:3</reference>; and שׁכן signifies to dwell, both inchoative: to come to dwell, and consecutive: to continue to dwell (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.15">Isa 57:15</reference>, of God who inhabiteth eternity). In general, the proverb means that the righteous fearlessly maintains the position he takes; while, on the contrary, all they who have no hold on God lose also their outward position. But often enough this saying is fulfilled in this, that they, in order that they may escape disgrace, became wanderers and fugitives, and are compelled to conceal themselves among strangers.
entries.796648988335aaee0a55f8ec0945307d1479f3c7: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.31">Pro 10:31</reference> <div eID="gen10951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10952" type="x-p"/> For the third time the favourite theme already handled in three appendixes is taken up: <div eID="gen10952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10953" type="x-p"/> The mouth of the righteous bringeth forth wisdom, <div eID="gen10953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10954" type="x-p"/> And the tongue of falsehood shall be rooted up. <div eID="gen10954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10955" type="x-p"/> Regarding the biblical comparison of thoughts with branches, and of words with flowers and fruits, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., my <hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. p. 181; and regarding the root נב (with its weaker אב), to swell up and to spring up (to well, grow, etc.), <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., what is said in the <hi type="italic">Comm. on Genesis</hi> on נביא, and in <hi type="italic">Isaiah</hi> on עוב. We use the word נוּב of that which sprouts or grows, and נבב of that which causes that something sprout; but also נוב may, after the manner of verbs of being full (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.10">Pro 3:10</reference>), of flowing (Gesen. §138, 1, Anm. 2), take the object accus. of that from which anything sprouts (<reference osisRef="Prov.24.31">Pro 24:31</reference>), or which sprouting, it raises up and brings forth (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.57.19">Isa 57:19</reference>). The mouth of the righteous sprouts, brings forth (in <reference osisRef="Ps.37.30">Psa 37:30</reference>, without a figure, יהגּה, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, utters) wisdom, which in all relations knows how to find out that which is truly good, and suitable for the end intended, and happily to unriddle difficult complications. The conception of wisdom, in itself practical (from חכם, to be thick = solid, firm), here gains such contents by the contrast: the tongue - whose character and fruit is falsehood, which has its delight in intentional perversions of fact, and thus increaseth complications (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding תּהפּכות, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.12">Pro 2:12</reference>) - is rooted up, whence it follows as regards the mouth of the righteous, that it continues for ever with that its wholesome fruit.
entries.e6a3285e8d4e6e411aa19d83dcce406da34a1592: <reference osisRef="Prov.10.32">Pro 10:32</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.10.32">32</reference> The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable;      But the mouth of the godless is mere falsehood. <div eID="gen10955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10956" type="x-p"/> Hitzig, instead of ידעוּן, reads יבּעוּן; the ἀποστάζει [they distil or send forth] of the lxx does not favour this, for it is probably only a corruption of ἐπίσταται, which is found in several MSS the <hi type="italic">Graec. Venet.</hi>, which translates ποιμανοῦσι, makes use of a MS which it sometimes misreads. The text does not stand in need of any emendations, but rather of a corrected relation between the clauses, for the relation of 31a with 32b, and of 32a with 31b, strongly commends itself (Hitzig); in that case the explanation lies near: the lips of the righteous find what is acceptable, viz., to God. But this thought in the Mashal language is otherwise expressed (<reference osisRef="Prov.12.2">Pro 12:2</reference> and paral.); and also 32a and 32b fit each other as contrasts, if by רצון, as <reference osisRef="Prov.11.27">Pro 11:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.14.9">Pro 14:9</reference>, is to be understood that which is acceptable in its widest generality, equally then in relation to God and man. It is a question whether ידעון means that they have knowledge of it (as one <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, says ידע ספר, to understand writing, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the reading of it), or that they think thereupon (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.27.23">Pro 27:23</reference>). Fundamentally the two ideas, according to the Hebrew conception of the words, lie in each other; for the central conception, perceiving, is biblically equivalent to a delighted searching into or going towards the object. Thus: the lips of the righteous think of that which is acceptable (רצון, cogn. to חן, gracefulness; χάρις, <reference osisRef="Col.4.6">Col 4:6</reference>); while the mouth of the godless is mere falsehood, which God (the wisdom of God) hates, and from which discord on all sides arises. We might transfer ידעון to 32b; but this line, interpreted as a clause by itself, is stronger and more pointed (Fl.).  <chapter eID="Prov.10"/> <div eID="gen10956" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:head>CHAP. X.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1. THe proverbs of <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Properly so called, for the foregoing Chapters, though they had this Title in the beginning of them, yet in truth were only a Preface or preparation to them, containing a general Exhortation to the study and exercise of wisdom, to stir up the minds of men to the greater attention and regard to all its Precepts, whereof some here follow. Of which in general these things are fit to be observed, to help us in the understanding of them: 1. That these sentences are generally distinct and independent, having no cohe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rence one with another, as many other parts of Scripture have: 2. That such sentences being very short, as their nature requires, more is understood in them than is expressed, and the Causes are commonly to be gathered from the Effects, and the Effects from the Causes, and one opposite from another, as we shall see. 3. That they are delivered by way of comparison and opposition, which for the most part is between Virtue and Vice, but sometimes is be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tween two Virtues, or two Vices.</ns0:note>. * A wise <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Prudent, and especially virtuous and godly, as this word is commonly meant in this Book, and in many other Scriptures.</ns0:note> son ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />keth<ns0:note place="margin">‖ Ch. 15. 20.</ns0:note> a glad father <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">And a glad Mother too; for both Parents are to be understood in both branches, as is evident from the nature of the thing which affects both of them, and from parallel places, as <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 17. 25. & 30. 17. although one only be ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pressed in each branch, for the greater Elegancy.</ns0:note>: but a foolish son <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the heaviness of his mother <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The occasi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on of her great sorrow, which is decently ascribed to the Mothers, rather than to the Fathers, because their passions are most vehe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment, and make deepest impression in them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 11. 4.</ns0:note> Treasures of Wickedness <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Either 1. All worldly Treasures and Riches, which are cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led the <ns0:hi>Mammon of Unrighteousness,</ns0:hi> Luke 16. 9. of which see the Reasons there, to which Righteousness or Holiness, which are spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ritual and heavenly Riches, may be fitly opposed. Or 2. Such Treasures as are got by any sort of unjust or wicked practices.</ns0:note> profit nothing <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">They do the possessor no good, but, which is implied from the opposite member, much hurt; they do not only not deliver him from death, but oft expose him to it, either from men, who take away his Life that they may enjoy his Wealth, or from God, who shortens his days, and makes his death more terrible, as being at<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tended with guilt, and with the second death.</ns0:note>: but righteousness <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Either 1. True Holiness of Heart and Life. Or 2. Justice and Equity in the get<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ting of Riches, or an Estate honestly obtained, which may be fitly opposed to <ns0:hi>Treasures of Wickedness.</ns0:hi> Or 3. A liberal and charitable use of Riches, which is oft called Righteousness, as <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 112. 9. <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 4. 27. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 9. 10. &c. and is indeed but an act of Justice, of which see on <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 3. 27. which also is conveniently opposed to an unjust getting of Riches; and so this contains a great Paradox, yet a certain truth, that the charitable laying out of Mony is more profitable to men than an unjust and covetous laying it up.</ns0:note> delivereth from death <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Oft times from temporal death, because men generally love, and ho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nour, and will assist such persons in cases of danger, and God gives them the blessing of a long Life; and always from eternal death, when such Charity proceeds from a sincere and honest mind, and a good Conscience.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 33. 19, & 37. 19, 25.</ns0:note> The LORD will not suffer the soul of the righ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />teous to famish <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Will preserve them from Famine, according to his Promises, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 34. 10. and elsewhere, which, as other temporal Promises, is not to be understood simply and universally, but with this limi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tation, except this be necessary for Gods Glory, which in all rea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son should over-rule the Creatures good, and for their own greater benefit. For to say nothing of eternal Felicities which follow eve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry good mans death, it is certainly in some times and cases, a less evil for men to be killed with Famine, than to survive to see and feel those miseries which are coming upon them, and upon the Land where they live.</ns0:note>: but he casteth away <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> the wick<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed for their wickedness.</ns0:note> the substance <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">As this word is used, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 52. 7. or <ns0:hi>the Wickedness, i. e.</ns0:hi> the wealth gotten by wickedness, as <ns0:hi>Righteousness, v.</ns0:hi> 2. is by divers understood of an Estate got with Righteousness.</ns0:note> of the wicked <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Who by that means shall be exposed to want and Famine.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 12 24. & 19. 15.</ns0:note> He becometh poor, that dealeth <ns0:hi>with</ns0:hi> a slack hand <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Negligently and slothfully, as appears from the <ns0:hi>diligence</ns0:hi> op<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />posed to it in the next branch, and from the use of this word in this sense, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 12. 24, 27. & 19. 15. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 48. 10. Heb. with <ns0:hi>a deceitful hand,</ns0:hi> so called, partly because it seems and pretends to do somthing, when in truth it doth nothing; and partly because such persons usually endeavour to maintain themselves by deceit and wickedness, which they cannot or will not do by honest labour and diligence.</ns0:note>: but <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 13. 4. & 21. 5.</ns0:note> the hand of the diligent maketh rich <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Not by it self, nor necessarily, as is manifest from Experience, and is noted, <ns0:hi>Eccles.</ns0:hi> 9. 11. but through Gods bles<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sing, which commonly is given to such, by comparing this verse with <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 22. here following.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5. He that gathereth <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">The fruits of his field.</ns0:note> in summer <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">In harvest, as it follows, which is a part of Summer. He that watcheth for and improveth the proper seasons and opportunities of doing good to himself, and to others.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> a wise son: <ns0:hi>but</ns0:hi> he that sleepeth in harvest <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> a son that causeth shame <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Both to himself for his folly, and that Poverty and Misery caused by it, and to his Parents, to whose negligent or evil Education such things are oft, and somtimes justly imputed.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6. Blessings <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> upon the head of the just <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">All sorts of blessings are wished to them by Men, and confer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />red upon them by God. He saith, <ns0:hi>upon</ns0:hi> their <ns0:hi>head,</ns0:hi> either to shew that these Blessings come from above: and that openly in the sight of the World, so that he can confidently speak of them to God's Praise, and to his own Comfort and Honour; or because Blessings were commonly pronounced by men with this Ceremony by lay<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing their hands upon the Head of the party blessed.</ns0:note>: but <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ver. 11.</ns0:note> violence covereth the mouth of the wicked <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Violence</ns0:hi> (either 1. Their own Violence or Injustice, which may be here put for the fruit or punishment of it, as <ns0:hi>Iniquity</ns0:hi> is oft put for the punishment of Iniquity. Or 2. Violence, or the violent and injurious, and mischievous practices of others against them, deserved by their own Violence committed against others, and inflicted upon them by the curse and righteous judgment of God) <ns0:hi>shall cover the mouth of the wicked, i. e.</ns0:hi> shall fall upon them. This Phrase of covering their Mouth, is used either 1. With allusion to the ancient custom of covering the Mouths and Faces of condemned Malefactors; of which see <ns0:hi>Esth.</ns0:hi> 7. 8. <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 9. 24. Or 2. To signifie that the Curse and Judg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment of God upon them should be so manifestly just, that their mouths should be stopped, and they not be able to speak a word a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gainst God, or for themselves. Or 3. to intimate that Gods judgment upon them should be publick and evident to all that be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hold them, as any covering put upon a mans mouth or Face is, as for the same reason the blessings of the just were said to be upon their Heads. And the <ns0:hi>Mouth</ns0:hi> may be put for the <ns0:hi>Face,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Counte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nance,</ns0:hi> by a <ns0:hi>Synecdoche:</ns0:hi> But this clause is otherwise rendred by di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vers learned Interpreters, <ns0:hi>the mouth of the wicked covereth (i. e.</ns0:hi> con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cealeth or smothereth within itself, and doth not utter that) <ns0:hi>vio<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lence</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>injury,</ns0:hi> which he meditateth in his Heart, and designeth to do to others, and therefore shall be accursed and miserable. But this suits not so well with the former clause, wherein the <ns0:hi>Blessings of the just</ns0:hi> are not meant actively of those Blessings which they wish or give to others, but passively of those Blessings which others wish or give to them, and consequently this <ns0:hi>violence</ns0:hi> is not understood of that which they do to others, but of that which is done to them by others.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 112. 6.</ns0:note> The memory of the just <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> blessed <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Honourable and acceptable to those who mention them. Compare <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 31. 20. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 62. 5.</ns0:note>: but the name of the wicked shall rot <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Shall perish, and be cursed and detestable amongst men, shall stink above ground.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8. The wise in heart will receive commandments <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Is ready to hear and obey the Counsels and Precepts of God and of Men, by which means he shall stand fast and live.</ns0:note>: but <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> a fool of lips.</ns0:note> a prating fool <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">One who is slow to hear, and swift to speak, who instead of receiving good Admonitions, Cavils, and Disputes against them. In the Hebrew he is called <ns0:hi>a fool of Lips,</ns0:hi> either because he discovers the folly of his Heart by his Lips, and thereby exposeth himself to the mischief here following, or because he is <ns0:hi>without heart,</ns0:hi> as is said of <ns0:hi>Ephraim, Hos.</ns0:hi> 7. 11. or, his <ns0:hi>Heart is little worth,</ns0:hi> as is said here, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 20. or because he speaks rashly without any consideration. Or, it may be rendred, <ns0:hi>a fool by his lips, i. e.</ns0:hi> by his foolish and wicked speeches, contrary to the commands of God, by talking much and ill, when it is more comely and necessary for him to hear and re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceive Instruction from others.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> shall be beaten.</ns0:note> shall fall <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">To wit, into mischief: or, <ns0:hi>be punished,</ns0:hi> as the word is used, <ns0:hi>Hos.</ns0:hi> 4. 14. or, <ns0:hi>be beaten,</ns0:hi> as below <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 10.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 23. 4.</ns0:note> He that walketh uprightly <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Who is sincere, and just, and faithful in his dealings with God and with men.</ns0:note>, walketh sure<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>securely,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>confidently,</ns0:hi> as the word properly signifies, and is here rendred by all the ancient Interpreters, and by most of the others, quietly resting upon Gods Favour, and gra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cious Providence for his Protection, and being supported by the Testimony of a good Conscience, and therefore not fearing nor caring who knows or observes his Actions, which he endeavours to approve both to God, and to men.</ns0:note>: but he that perverteth his ways <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">That walks perversly, or frowardly, or in crooked and sinful paths, that dealeth hypocriti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cally and deceitfully with God, or with men, using all possible crafts to conceal his wickedness.</ns0:note> shall be known <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">His wickedness shall be pub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lickly discovered, and so he shall be exposed to all that shame and punishment which his sins deserve, and which he thought by his cunning practices to avoid.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 6. 13.</ns0:note> He that winketh with the eye <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">That secretly and cunningly designs mischiefs against others, as this Phrase is used, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 35. 19. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 6. 13.</ns0:note> causeth sor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />row <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">To others, and afterwards to himself.</ns0:note>: but <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>and,</ns0:hi> as it is in the Hebrew: for vice is not here opposed to virtue, as it is in many other Proverbs, but one vice is compared with another.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ver. 8.</ns0:note> a prating fool <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Who is so far from such deceits, that he runs into the other extream, and <ns0:hi>uttereth all his mind,</ns0:hi> as is said of the Fool, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 29. 11. and thereby speaks ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ny things offensive to others, and mischievous to himself.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> shall be beaten.</ns0:note> shall fall.</ns0:p>
